messages.subject: [S] confidence intervals vs likelihood ratios: a math-stats query
messages.subject_clean: [S] confidence intervals vs likelihood ratios: a math-stats query
messages.body_plain:
Consider a multiple regression model. There are two measures 
of the signficance of a particular parameter \beta_i.

One may test the hypothesis that the true value of
the parameter is zero by assuming that 

        (\beta_i - \hat{\beta_i})/ s.e(\hat{\beta_i}) ~ N(0,1)

that is, generate a z-statistic from the parameter estimate and
its estimated variance, which is a normal approximation of a student
approximation of the actual simultaneous confidence interval.

Another test is the likelihood ratio test on nested models, with the
submodel having \beta_i = 0.

Can anyone tell me, or point me to a reference, which explains,
the relationship and difference between these two tests? My
source on the subject (Johnson and Wichern) baldly introduces the
two notions (CI and likelihood ratios) one after the other, but
does not indicate the relation, unless its supposed to be obvious
from the algebra.

Thanks in advance.

Steve

Dear Hong Ooi,

Thanks for your prompt reply, but that was the part i figured out myself.
Maybe my real question is: how were the values of 1, 1, 0, 0.5, 1, and 1
calculated. According to the manuals of splus the dissimilarity between
two binary values is calculated as (a + b)/(a + b + c + d) where a and b
are the cases in which
the objects are not identical for a particular variable. Using this
formula I would obtain a dissimilarity 2/5=0.4 for object 1 and 2 instead
of 1.0. What am i doing wrong?

Antoine

Hong Ooi wrote:

> On Tue, 01 Aug 2000 13:51:26 +0100, "A.H.C. van Kampen"

> diagonal of the (symmetric) distance matrix

>   1  0.5  0

Re: (S) confidence intervals vs likelihood ratios: a math-st
     by Steve Cumming
     
     One simple difference between LR, LM and Wald-Tests on the one hand 
     and the confidence intervalls (or Hartley-Test or a test via 
     Chebyshev's inequality) on the other hand is that the former tests 
     obviously apply also to non-linear hypotheses.
     
     If any list member knows more about the performance of those linear 
     and non-linear test statistics in small samples I would be interested 
     too.
     
     References (from the econometrics corner only and maybe somewhat out 
     of date):
     
     Judge, Griffiths, Hill, Lütkepohl, Lee (Ch. 6.5 to 6.8)
     "The Theory and Practice of Econometrics"
     Wiley 1985
     (see also references cited there, i.e. Gallant '75 for a MC-evaluation 
     of various test statistics)
     
     Amemiya 1983, "Nonlinear Regression Models"
     in Handbook of Econometrics
     Ed. Griliches, Intriligator, North-Holland
     
     Regards
     Thomas Siwik

messages.body_plain:
Some general comments about LR vs Wald CIs

For linear models and linear hypotheses there is not much difference between
the methods in finite samples and asymptotically. However, for nonlinear
hypotheses (hypotheses about nonlinear functions of the parameters. For
example HO: g(b) = b1/b2 = 1 vs H1: g(b) = b1/b2 /= 1) there can be very
great differences between LR and Wald CIs in finite samples. The big problem
with Wald-based CIs is that they are not invariate to how the nonlinear
hypothesis is formulated. In the previous example, one can get numerically
different results and different conclusions if the hypothesis is
reparameterized as g(b) = b1 - b2 = 0. The LR CI, however, is invariant to
the parameterization of the nonlinear hypothesis and is much more reliable,
in general. Jean-Marie Dufour at University of Montreal (econometrician) has
written several papers slamming the Wald test. ez

I'm running a series of simple bivariate linear regressions on grouped 
data.  I want to test the slopes to see if they are parallel.  I normally 
use analysis of covariance to do so, looking at interaction between the 
covariate and the grouping factor to make this determination.

VR3 pp.149 - 154 has a very nice example of an ANCOVA, ending with a 
discussion of this very operation.  It includes a note to change the 
contrast parametrization beforehand.  (I did learn that SPlus and R use 
different default parametrization).

My question has to do with the issue of parametrization.  The interaction 
term doesn't appear to change regardless of the parametrization.  Since the 
significance or non-significance of the interaction is all that is relevant 
to the question of parallel slopes, does it really matter what

messages.subject: [S] summary - detecting data precision
messages.body_plain:
I had posted, "I would like to determine the maximum precision of a vector".

Longhow - thank you so much, your suggestion to convert to a character vector
was better than the loopy things I was envisioning.

All - I extended Longhow's suggestion, the function below works for numbers on
either side of the decimal.

percision.digit <- function(x){
   if(any(trunc(x)!=x, na.rm=T)){
     x.char <- format(na.omit(x))
     x.period <- regexpr("\\.", x.char)
     x.length <- nchar(x.char[1])
     x.res <- x.length - x.period[1]
   }
   else{
     x.char <- as.character(na.omit(x))
     x.zero <- unlist(attributes(regexpr('0+', x.char)))
     x.res <- ifelse(min(x.zero) == -1, 0, min(x.zero)*-1)
   }
   x.res
}

# demo
> percision.digit(3)
[1] 0
> percision.digit(33300)
[1] -2
> percision.digit(333)
[1] 0
> percision.digit(0.333)
[1] 3
> percision.digit(0.00333)
[1] 5

# in use
> x <- c(195, 4.3, 0.7)
> mean(x, na.rm = T)
[1] 66.66667
> round(mean(x, na.rm = T), percision.digit(x) + 1)
[1] 66.67
# note - signif() could have been used, but only if you know what to set the
   argument digit equal to

I chose to use round as I'm assuming the data are reported in units reflective
   of the resolution of the measuring instrument.

Thanks, KJJ

messages.subject: Re: [S] Breslow Day Statistic
messages.body_plain:
Hopefully, the answer to the question is NO. ("Has anybody written a
function to calculate the Breslow-Day statistic?")

As Norman Breslow took pains to point out in his plenary address ('The
R.A. Fisher Lecture') at the JSM a few years back, the 'Breslow-Day' test
is incorrect. 

The preferred test is due to Tarone (1985 Biometrika, 72:91-95).

AFAIK, this test is not in Splus and not apparent in Statlib's S Archive.
But tests of homogeneity of odds are available via loglin() and glm().

messages.subject: Re: [S] omitting some observations in anova
messages.body_plain:
Dear Andrew

> if i find that some observations in the data
> set do not represent useful data and should
> be excluded, is there any way in splus i can
> omit these observations and carry out anova
> as per usual.

If you're only deleting the observations because they might distort
the usual ANOVA analysis, it may be better to  retain the observations, 
preserving the symmetry & balance of the original experimental design, 
and instead to adopt a different method of analysis of variance.
There are 'robust' methods which are designed to be insensitive to outliers
etc. An example is median polishing (explained in Venables & Ripley chapter 8).
There is a robust version of 'lm' called 'rlm' in the MASS library 
(last time I looked!) and some of the other Splus functions have a "robust" or
"quasi" option that can be given as the distribution family argument.

regards
Adrian
----

                <http://maths.uwa.edu.au/~adrian/>

messages.subject: Re: [S] second - > date
messages.body_plain:
On Thu, 3 Aug 2000, Mathieu Ros wrote:

> In order not to re-invent the wheel, I have a question about date handling.
> I have dates in seconds which I'd like to convert in DD/MM/YY-HH/MM/SS
> format (for day/month/year-hour/minits/seconds) in order to use them in time
> series.

Three potential problems:

1) I presume you know the origin (seconds past what)?

2) Timezones.  Timezones can do *really* complicated things, especially
if the times are not recent ones.

3) Leap seconds. Not all days are the same length.

I would code up some C code to do the conversions (on a POSIX system times
are seconds since the beginning of 1970), as the details are really messy.  
strftime(localtime()) will do the conversions from seconds to ascii in
various ways. 

The chron library (or at least the version I last looked at, which is a lot
later than those supplied with S-PLUS) will get this approximately right
(no timezones, no leap seconds) if you divide seconds by 86400 to get
`days'. Probably fine for recent times in UTC (formerly GMT).

You don't say what version of S-PLUS you have (but I seem to recall you use
2000).  5.x has various calendar functions which may help.  Start with
?timeSeries.

--

messages.subject: [S] Preventing overfitting artefacts in mulitiple linear regression
messages.subject_clean: [S] Preventing overfitting artefacts in mulitiple linear regression
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
    I have constructed a multiple linear regression model with four
factors X1-X4 implemented in S-Plus as

             initial.lm.object <- glm(Y ~ X1 * X2 * X3 * X4)

I allow interaction among factors (denoted by * in the above
expression), because that makes for a better fit (not just in terms of
larger R^2 values, see below).   However, as you can see, this also
makes for a rather large number of factors in the model.  I use Mallows'
Cp index to weed out the factors that do not substantially improve the
fit of the model to the data, using the expression

            final.lm.object<-step(initial.lm.object)

This  tends to retain a total of six to eight factors in the final model
(I fit the model individually to many independent data sets, ie, the
responses of individual brain cells.  Hence the best-fitting model
differs from one cell to the next).   This final model also produces
high R^2 values (0.80-0.99), as well as highly significant p values in
the F-test.  The residuals are normally distributed.  I get similar
results when I use leaps() insted of step() to whittle down the model.

        However, many of my colleague still argue that the good fits are
an artefact of overfitting resulting from having from too many factors.
I explain to them how the Mallows' index works, but they're still not
satisfied.  So I'd like to run one or more additional tests to address
the overfitting concerns before submitting my manuscript describing
these results.

        So my questions are:
        (a)  Which test/s best complement the Mallows' Cp criterion in
terms of checking for overfitting?
        (b)  Do you know if they're implemented in S-Plus?
        (c)  I know that evaluating models is often a matter of
judgement, but am I missing any other test/s that are obviously
necessary?

        Thank you in advance,
        Jay Hegde
        Washington University School of Medicine, Box 8108
        St. Louis, MO 63110
        jay at v1.wustl.edu

Jay - a couple of issues.  First, using the data to guide model
selection can result in a simpler model but its worth can be
illusory.  Model uncertainty causes falsely narrow confidence
limits, inflated adjusted R^2, falsely low P-values and standard
errors, and biases in beta-hat.  Once you allow for interactions,
statistical inference and estimation can be distorted if you then
decide to remove interaction terms.  Second, any term selection
that you do is be do to in a hierarchical manner, i.e., force in
lower order terms when considering a higher order one - you may
be doing this already.  Third, a totally different approach that
has some advantages is to use penalized maximum likelihood estimation
to penalize complex terms (e.g., interactions) more than simpler
terms (e.g., main effects and lower order interactions).  For the
last concept see my 1998 Statistics in Medicine paper.  A good
reference for model uncertainty is 

@ARTICLE{cha95mod,
  author = {Chatfield, C.},
  year = 1995,
  title = {Model uncertainty, data mining and statistical inference
(with
          discussion)},
  journal = JRSSA,
  volume = 158,
  pages = {419-466},
  annote = {bias by selecting model because it fits the data well; bias
in
           standard errors;P. 420: ... need for a better balance in the
           literature and in statistical teaching between {\em
techniques} and
           problem solving {\em strategies}. P. 421: It is `well known'
to be
           `logically unsound and practically misleading' (Zhang, 1992)
to
           make inferences as if a model is known to be true when it
has, in
           fact, been selected from the {\em same} data to be used for
           estimation purposes. However, although statisticians may
admit this
           privately (Breiman (1992) calls it a `quiet scandal'), they
(we)
           continue to ignore the difficulties because it is not clear
what
           else could or should be done. P. 421: Estimation errors for
           regression coefficients are usually smaller than errors from
           failing to take into account model specification. P. 422:
           Statisticians must stop pretending that model uncertainty
does not
           exist and begin to find ways of coping with it. P. 426: It is
           indeed strange that we often admit model uncertainty by
searching
           for a best model but then ignore this uncertainty by making
           inferences and predictions as if certain that the best
fitting
           model is actually true. P. 427: The analyst needs to assess
the
           model selection {\em process} and not just the best fitting
model.
           P. 432: The use of subset selection methods is well known to
           introduce alarming biases. P. 433: ... the AIC can be highly
biased
           in data-driven model selection situations. P. 434: Prediction
           intervals will generally be too narrow. In the discussion,
Jamal R.
           M. Ameen states that a model should be (a) satisfactory in
           performance relative to the stated objective, (b) logically
sound,
           (c) representative, (d) questionable and subject to on-line
           interrogation, (e) able to accommodate external or expert
           information and (f) able to convey information.}

messages.subject: RE: [S] Preventing overfitting artefacts in multiple linear regression
messages.subject_clean: [S] Preventing overfitting artefacts in multiple linear regression
messages.body_plain:
Prof Harrell,

A few points from an econometrician (applied) of 25+ years experience:

0. Log-linear relationships may fit behavior better than linear ones. This
is surely true in the economic sciences, especially in the stimulus-response
cases. Second order log linear models such as cost functions and input
demand models, and customer demand studies for related goods are excellent
examples. There are several volumes of the handbook of econometrics ed. by
Z. Griliches and M. Intriligator, Elsevier/North-Holland that may help. Take
a guide through that swamp, however.
1. As jay suggested, just putting in 2nd order terms because they improve
the model is dangerous. Best if you have some explicit mechanism from theory
to justify inclusion of second order interactions.
2. There is a school of thought in some social science research that 2nd
order terms may appear correctly when first order effects are zero IF the
subject term is a mediator of the effects of another term in the model.
3. Overfitting tests can sometimes tell you if you are badly astray. But
they may indicate only that you lack sufficient observations to sort out the
underlying relationships. Ultimately there is no substitute for theory, tho
in the dark ages, step-wise regression was treated as such. (Some
epidemiology studies were awful in this way.)
4. Where possible, try to find multiple relationships that incorporate some
of the same independent variables. Simultaneous estimation of related
equations (by some variant of GLS) sometimes helps clarify the true
relationships in each.
5. I have a colleague at Rensselaer, Richard Burke (burker at rpi.edu) who has
worked in bio- and health statistics. You may want to get his comments. I
don't think he is an splus adherent, so he may not receive s-news.
6. "Artefact" is allowable, but "artifact" is preferred. (Couldn't resist.
Sorry.)

As usual, and as jay suggests, this stuff is deeper than it appears at
first. Good answers are defensible ones in the context of your study.

Regards
Randy Norsworthy

John R. Norsworthy
Professor of Economics and Finance
Lally School of Management and Technology
 and Faculty of Information Technology
Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute
Troy NY 12180 USA
Phone 518 276-6649
e-mail norswj at rpi.edu

jay wrote:
>
> Hi,
>     I have constructed a multiple linear regression model with four
> factors X1-X4 implemented in S-Plus as
>
>              initial.lm.object <- glm(Y ~ X1 * X2 * X3 * X4)
>
> I allow interaction among factors (denoted by * in the above
> expression), because that makes for a better fit (not just in terms of
> larger R^2 values, see below).   However, as you can see, this also
> makes for a rather large number of factors in the model.  I use Mallows'
> Cp index to weed out the factors that do not substantially improve the
> fit of the model to the data, using the expression
>
>             final.lm.object<-step(initial.lm.object)
>
> This  tends to retain a total of six to eight factors in the final model
> (I fit the model individually to many independent data sets, ie, the
> responses of individual brain cells.  Hence the best-fitting model
> differs from one cell to the next).   This final model also produces
> high R^2 values (0.80-0.99), as well as highly significant p values in
> the F-test.  The residuals are normally distributed.  I get similar
> results when I use leaps() insted of step() to whittle down the model.
>
>         However, many of my colleague still argue that the good fits are
> an artefact of overfitting resulting from having from too many factors.
> I explain to them how the Mallows' index works, but they're still not
> satisfied.  So I'd like to run one or more additional tests to address
> the overfitting concerns before submitting my manuscript describing
> these results.
>
>         So my questions are:
>         (a)  Which test/s best complement the Mallows' Cp criterion in
> terms of checking for overfitting?
>         (b)  Do you know if they're implemented in S-Plus?
>         (c)  I know that evaluating models is often a matter of
> judgement, but am I missing any other test/s that are obviously
> necessary?
>
>         Thank you in advance,
>         Jay Hegde
>         Washington University School of Medicine, Box 8108
>         St. Louis, MO 63110
>         jay at v1.wustl.edu
>

> send e-mail to s-news-request at wubios.wustl.edu with the BODY of the
> message:  unsubscribe s-news

Jay - a couple of issues.  First, using the data to guide model
selection can result in a simpler model but its worth can be
illusory.  Model uncertainty causes falsely narrow confidence
limits, inflated adjusted R^2, falsely low P-values and standard
errors, and biases in beta-hat.  Once you allow for interactions,
statistical inference and estimation can be distorted if you then
decide to remove interaction terms.  Second, any term selection
that you do is be do to in a hierarchical manner, i.e., force in
lower order terms when considering a higher order one - you may
be doing this already.  Third, a totally different approach that
has some advantages is to use penalized maximum likelihood estimation
to penalize complex terms (e.g., interactions) more than simpler
terms (e.g., main effects and lower order interactions).  For the
last concept see my 1998 Statistics in Medicine paper.  A good
reference for model uncertainty is

@ARTICLE{cha95mod,
  author = {Chatfield, C.},
  year = 1995,
  title = {Model uncertainty, data mining and statistical inference
(with
          discussion)},
  journal = JRSSA,
  volume = 158,
  pages = {419-466},
  annote = {bias by selecting model because it fits the data well; bias
in
           standard errors;P. 420: ... need for a better balance in the
           literature and in statistical teaching between {\em
techniques} and
           problem solving {\em strategies}. P. 421: It is `well known'
to be
           `logically unsound and practically misleading' (Zhang, 1992)
to
           make inferences as if a model is known to be true when it
has, in
           fact, been selected from the {\em same} data to be used for
           estimation purposes. However, although statisticians may
admit this
           privately (Breiman (1992) calls it a `quiet scandal'), they
(we)
           continue to ignore the difficulties because it is not clear
what
           else could or should be done. P. 421: Estimation errors for
           regression coefficients are usually smaller than errors from
           failing to take into account model specification. P. 422:
           Statisticians must stop pretending that model uncertainty
does not
           exist and begin to find ways of coping with it. P. 426: It is
           indeed strange that we often admit model uncertainty by
searching
           for a best model but then ignore this uncertainty by making
           inferences and predictions as if certain that the best
fitting
           model is actually true. P. 427: The analyst needs to assess
the
           model selection {\em process} and not just the best fitting
model.
           P. 432: The use of subset selection methods is well known to
           introduce alarming biases. P. 433: ... the AIC can be highly
biased
           in data-driven model selection situations. P. 434: Prediction
           intervals will generally be too narrow. In the discussion,
Jamal R.
           M. Ameen states that a model should be (a) satisfactory in
           performance relative to the stated objective, (b) logically
sound,
           (c) representative, (d) questionable and subject to on-line
           interrogation, (e) able to accommodate external or expert
           information and (f) able to convey information.}

--
Frank E Harrell Jr              Prof. of Biostatistics & Statistics
Div. of Biostatistics & Epidem. Dept. of Health Evaluation Sciences
U. Virginia School of Medicine  http://hesweb1.med.virginia.edu/biostat

messages.body_plain:
On Fri, 4 Aug 2000, Gerrit Eichner wrote:

> 
> Hello everybody,
> 
> I couldn't figure out a way to do the following:
> 
> Say, I have a list ll with named components and I want to use lapply to
> apply a function f to the components of the list. Within f I want to know
> the name of the component to which f is currently applied (to do some
> plotting or printing, say, at that very moment):
> 
> ll <- list(a=<something>, b=<something similar>, c=<similar>)
> 
> lapply(ll, function(x) {Do something with x and, e. g., print the name of
>                       the currently treated ll-component.})
> 
> Of course, within the function x does not have the original component's 
> name anymore. Does anybody know a way to retrieve this name *within* the

No, but you can apply lapply or sapply to the names of the list rather than
the list itself, along the lines of

lapply(names(ll), function(x) {access ll[[x]] or name x}

Your list better have names for this to work, and you can also use

lapply(seq(along=ll), function(x) {access ll[[x]] or names(ll)[x]}

to index by number.

Brian Ripley's answer:
**********************
No, but you can apply lapply or sapply to the names of the list rather than
the list itself, along the lines of

lapply(names(ll), function(x) {access ll[[x]] or name x}

Your list better have names for this to work, and you can also use

Tillmann Krahnke's answer:

m2 <- list(x =1:3, y=5:7)
attr(m2, "MyLabel" ) <- "Label 2"
mylist <- list(a = m1 , b = m2)
invisible(lapply(mylist, function(x) {print(attr(x, "MyLabel")); plot(x,
xlab= attr(x, "MyLabel"))} ))

messages.subject: [S] Overfitting and R-square
messages.body_plain:
Joseph Lucke sent a comment to me that encouraged me to elaborate
on my statement that adjusted R-square is inflated due to overfitting.
The correct statement is that adjusted R^2 is a good estimate of
the likely future performance of the model if you fit a SINGLE
pre-specified model.  If a series of models is entertained, and
especially if the final model is chosen on the basis of the sum
of squared errors or some related statistic, adj R^2 is no longer
a nearly-unbiased estimate.  The problem is that most people and
all software packages use as the regression degrees of freedom in
the formula the number of slopes in the FINAL model.  Copas,
Spiegelhalter, van Houwelingen and le Cessie, Ye and others have 
shown that it's much closer to the truth to use the maximum d.f. 
entertained.  Once you do that you see that very little is
gained by simplifying the model purely on the basis of the data,
unless something akin to differential penalization or Bayesian
techniques are used.
An exception to that is when the terms removed from the model
are clearly complete noise and the remaining terms are very important.
So adj. R^2 as it is commonly used is inflated due to overfitting.
Similar problems exist when using Cp or AIC for more than
2 possible models.

The clearest way I can think of for studying this problem is to
consider in the context of least squares multiple regression the
problem of estimating the residual variance sigma^2.  What is an
unbiased estimate?  One is SSE/(n-p-1) where p=# parameters in
the pre-specified full model aside from the intercept and SSE
is the sum of squared errors from that model.  If model selection
is done, one tries to keep SSE from increasing much but one tries
to decrease p significantly.  This results in a seriously biased
sigma^2 estimate if one uses SSE and p from the "final" model.
Ye (JASA 1998) has developed a data-mining-adjusted estimate of
sigma^2 that uses SSE from the final model and n-gdf-1 where
the generalized d.f. gdf turns out to be remarkably close to
p from the full model and remarkably larger than p from the
reduced model.  Is statistics fun or what?

Larry Freedman showed that stepwise variable selection can be
made safer if one uses as sigma^2 the estimate from the 
full model and not that from the current model.
-- 
Frank E Harrell Jr              Prof. of Biostatistics & Statistics
Div. of Biostatistics & Epidem. Dept. of Health Evaluation Sciences
U. Virginia School of Medicine  http://hesweb1.med.virginia.edu/biostat

messages.subject: Re: [S] summary: list's component name within fct. within lapply
messages.subject_clean: [S] summary: list's component name within fct. within lapply
messages.body_plain:
I have found handy a little function in the Hmisc library
called llist.

llist <- function(..., labels=T) {
  dotlist <- list(...)
  lname <- names(dotlist)
  name <- vname <- as.character(sys.call()[-1])
  for(i in 1:length(dotlist)) {
        vname[i] <- lname[i]
        if(length(vname[i])==0 || vname[i]=='') vname[i] <- name[i]
        lab <- vname[i]
        if(labels) {
          lab <- attr(dotlist[[i]],'label')
          if(length(lab) == 0) lab <- vname[i]
        } 
        label(dotlist[[i]]) <- lab
  }
  names(dotlist) <- vname[1:length(dotlist)]
  dotlist
}
  
`llist' is like `list' except that it preserves the names or labels
of the component variables in the variables `label' attribute.  This can
be useful when looping over variables or using `sapply' or `lapply'. By
using 
`llist' instead of `list' one can annotate the output with the current 
variable's name or label.  `llist' also defines a `names' attribute for
the list and pulls the `names' from the arguments' expressions for
non-named arguments.

.AG labels
set to `F' to make `llist' ignore the variables' `label' attribute and
use the variables' names.

##In these examples of llist, note that labels are printed after
##variable names, because of print.labelled
a <- 1:3
b <- 4:6
label(b) <- 'B Label'
llist(a,b)
$a:
a 
[1] 1 2 3

$b:
b 
[1] 4 5 6

llist(a,b,d=0)
$a:
a 
[1] 1 2 3

$b:
B Label 
[1] 4 5 6

$d:
d 
[1] 0

llist(a,b,0)
$a:
a 
[1] 1 2 3

$b:
B Label 
[1] 4 5 6

$"0":
0 
[1] 0

w <- llist(a, b>5, d=101:103)
sapply(w, function(x){
  hist(x)
  title(label(x))
  locator(1)   ## wait for mouse click
})

#OR:
for(u in w) {hist(u); title(label(u))}

NOTE THAT llist needs the label function in Hmisc
(which is quite a trivial function).

Gerrit Eichner wrote:
> 
> Hi!
> 
> Thanks to Brian Ripley and Tillmann Krahnke who responded quickly and pro-
> vided an answer to my question. I've appended their suggestions below.
> 
> (I had tackled the problem (quite crudely!) by "re-packing" the list such
> that each component was replaced by a list comprising this component and
> its original name. So, in a way I duplicated the components' names.
> Tillmann's idea is comparable to this method. However, I think, Brian's
> proposal, esp. the second, is the most "natural" way to do it.)
> 
>  Best regards  --  Gerrit
> 
>  -------------------------------------------------------------------------
>   Gerrit Eichner                            Mathematical Institute of the
>   gerrit.eichner at math.uni-giessen.de        Justus-Liebig-Univ. Giessen
>   Tel: +49-(0)641-99-32104                  Arndtstr. 2, D-35392 Giessen
>   Fax: +49-(0)641-99-32029        http://www.uni-giessen.de/AG_Stochastik
>  -------------------------------------------------------------------------
> 
> Original question:
> ******************
> > Say, I have a list ll with named components and I want to use lapply to
> > apply a function f to the components of the list. Within f I want to know
> > the name of the component to which f is currently applied (to do some
> > plotting or printing, say, at that very moment):
> >
> > ll <- list(a=<something>, b=<something similar>, c=<similar>)
> >
> > lapply(ll, function(x) {Do something with x and, e. g., print the name of
> >                       the currently treated ll-component.})
> >
> > Of course, within the function x does not have the original component's
> > name anymore. Does anybody know a way to retrieve this name *within* the
> > function?
> 
> Brian Ripley's answer:
> **********************
> No, but you can apply lapply or sapply to the names of the list rather than
> the list itself, along the lines of
> 
> lapply(names(ll), function(x) {access ll[[x]] or name x}
> 
> Your list better have names for this to work, and you can also use
> 
> lapply(seq(along=ll), function(x) {access ll[[x]] or names(ll)[x]}
> 
> to index by number.
> 
> Tillmann Krahnke's answer:
> *************************
> you can add a new attribute to the list elements which consists of the
> elements' names (or some Labels, which is what I did) and use this in
> lapply:
> 
> (Note that I included lapply() in invisble() to avoid printout of the
> names of the elements of "mylist")
> 
> m1 <- 1:3
> attr(m1, "MyLabel") <- "Label 1"
> m2 <- list(x =1:3, y=5:7)
> attr(m2, "MyLabel" ) <- "Label 2"
> mylist <- list(a = m1 , b = m2)
> invisible(lapply(mylist, function(x) {print(attr(x, "MyLabel")); plot(x,
> xlab= attr(x, "MyLabel"))} ))
>

messages.body_plain:
Dear S+ Users

I still feel as an S+ true beginner

My problem is a little complex and I hope I will explain it as clearly as 
possible.

I am using S+2000 on a Win95 platform.

I am analysing data of female fecundity of a sea lice parasitic on flatfishes.

I have to regress counts of eggs (Neggs) against various factors/variables, 
with a relation of the form:

Neggs= NParasites + HostLenth + HostCondition + Year + Month + Boat

However NParasites (counts of parasites) also is dependent on the others

I thus plan to correct this effect  using the residuals of a regression of 
the type :

NParasites = HostLenth + HostCondition + Year + Month + Boat

Is this correct? (I would not see why not but after all I am not a 
satistical hero)

However this would be fair enough if the effective relationships between 
NParasites and HostLenth and HostCondition were linear or at least 
monotonous. On the contrary the relashionships are bell shaped (maximum of 
parasites for medium sized hosts or medium healthy hosts) and the data are 
completely overdispersed (as usual for parasites counts against host size)

Thus I chose to use the gam regression using spine function and the 
following synthax:

gamb1<-gam(formula = ZO ~ s(Length) + Month +
        Year + s(K) + Boat, family = quasi(
        link = log, variance = "mu"), data
        = AbB959699, na.action =
        na.exclude, control = list(epsilon
        = 0.001, bf.epsilon = 0.001,
        maxit = 50, bf.maxit = 10, trace
        = F))
(ZO is a parasite count on a particular location on the host)

Is this correct?

This way S+ only provides testing for non-linear terms. Why?

I then wanted to get the simplest model (e.g. Boat, a categorical factor, 
does not seem to do much)

Using "step" I got:

Error in step.gam(gamb1): you must supply a scope argument to step.gam(); 
the gam.scope() function might be useful

I then tried the gam.scope(gamb1) but could not figure out the results and 
then tried the following:

step(gamb1,scope=list("Length"~1+s(Length), "Month"~1+Month, "Year"~1+Year, 
"K"~1+s(K), "Boat"~1+Boat))

and obtained this

Start:  ZO ~ s(Length) + Month + Year + s(K) + Boat; AIC= 673.749
Trial:  ZO ~  1 + Month + Year + s(K) + Boat; AIC= 677.1291

Trial:  ZO ~  s(Length) + Month + Year + s(K) + 1; AIC= 644.4642
Step :  ZO ~ s(Length) + Month + Year + s(K) ; AIC= 644.4642

Trial:  ZO ~  1 + Month + Year + s(K) + 1; AIC= 643.6964

Trial:  ZO ~  s(Length) + 1 + Year + s(K) + 1; AIC= 640.28

Trial:  ZO ~  s(Length) + Month + 1 + s(K) + 1; AIC= 652.1901

Trial:  ZO ~  s(Length) + Month + Year + 1 + 1; AIC= 640.7583

Trial:  ZO ~  s(Length) + Month + Year + s(K) + "Boat"Error in 
step.gam(gamb1, scope = list("Length" ~ 1 + s(Le

ngth), "..: Length of variable 6 is 1 != length of row names (482)

How do I interpret this error message? What should be done?

Boat could (or should) be safely rejected (apparently)

May I retrieve the residuals of the complete model without caring of these 
problems?

Thank you a lot if some one can help me

Sincerely

Thierry

messages.subject: [S] summary v. quantile (simple question)
messages.body_plain:
S+ 2000 R2 on Win NT 4.0 SP6

I apologize in advance if this is a trivial question.  The variable x is a
sequence of four digit years.  The original file from which this variable
was extracted is a MS Access database.  The following rounding behavior
seems unusual and I have not been able to identify the cause.  summary()
applied to the variable in the datasheet has an identical result to
summary(x).

> table(x)
 1986 1987 1988 1989 1990 1991 1992 1993 1994 1995 1996 1997 
 2600 2640 2942 3163 3112 3195 3576 3350 3162 2399 1697  867

> attr(x)
NULL

> data.class(x)
[1] "numeric"

> summary(x)
 Min. 1st Qu. Median Mean 3rd Qu. Max. 
 1990    1990   1990 1990    1990 2000

> quantile(x)
   0%  25%  50%  75% 100% 
 1986 1988 1991 1993 1997

When using the dialog box for summary statistics I get:

     Min:  1986.0000
 1st Qu.:  1988.0000
    Mean:  1991.0373
  Median:  1991.0000
 3rd Qu.:  1993.0000
     Max:  1997.0000
 Total N: 32703.0000
   NA's :     0.0000
Std Dev.:     3.0634

which is consistent with quantile.  Any ideas/explanations would be greatly
appreciated.

K

messages.subject: [S] Problem subsetting a matrix element from data frame
messages.subject_clean: [S] Problem subsetting a matrix element from data frame
messages.body_plain:
I have encountered the following problem on S-Plus 6.0 beta 1 on Linux.
I am sending this to s-news because I assume the problem also exists
on S-Plus 5.1.

I routinely attach a label attribute to variables and use a new
class 'labelled' for this to handle printing and subsetting.  Here
is the subsetting function I use for elements of class 'labelled':

"[.labelled"<- function(x, ...) {
  lab <- attr(x, "label")
  x <- NextMethod("[")
  attr(x, "label") <- lab
  if(!inherits(x,'labelled'))
    attr(x,'class') <- c("labelled", attr(x,'class'))
  x
}

When I construct a data frame containing a matrix element of class
'labelled', subsetting the resulting data frame causes the
matrix aspect of the 2nd element to be ignored.  This happens in
the above NextMethod("[") command.  The following commands create
the test data (please no comments about the possibly non-future-

> >   x <- NextMethod("[")
> >   attr(x, "label") <- lab

messages.subject: [S] summary: algorithm used in smooth()
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

Last week I posted a question about what exact algorithm is used in the
function "smooth".  The help file says it uses "4(3RSR)2H", but I couldn't
find the notations in the references cited.  Thanks to responses from Colin
Mallows and Bill Dunlap, I think it means:

Running medians of 4; ("4")
Running medians of 3; ("3") repeated until convergence ("R")
Splitting ("S") repeated until convergence ("R")
Running medians of 2 ("2")
Hanning ("H")

The mystery remains as to what the parentheses around 3RSR means.  Bill
Dunlap conjectured that it's only there to separate the "4" and "3"; i.e.,
to make it clear that they are separate operations.

messages.subject: [S] trellis histogram with superposed line - solution
messages.subject_clean: [S] trellis histogram with superposed line - solution
messages.body_plain:
Last week I posted the question of how to superpose a vertical line on to a
trellis histogram. I had two responses, one by James Pratt and the second by
Michael Bramley). The solution that worked best for me was provided by James
Pratt (Sonus Pharmaceuticals) (jimp at sonuspharma.com)

.....

xx is a dataframe with resp (normal variates about 10 different means), grp
(a factor with 10 levels), and m2 is a vector external to xx with values at
the true means where I'd like a vertical line drawn within each panel.

m2 is used in the histogram call by naming it vref.  Since within histogram
function, the argument list contains the ... argument, you can pass anything
else along and use it in your defined panel function (but must use the same
name, vref in this case).  vref is passed to the defined panel function in
its entirety, so must subscript it somehow by knowing which panel are in so
know what value to draw line at.  This was a tricky part, but noticed that
subscirpts vector within each panel was 1:46 or 47:92, ... .  This is due to
the nint=45 argument.  I found this out by placing a print(subscripts) call
within the panel function.  Based on this information, I modfied the
panel.abline call.  If one uses a different nint value, then need to
correspondingly change the panel.abline call (the divisor of 46 would need
to be changed to nint+1.  [The second version below tries to do this, but
not yet in a totally automatic way.  You can't just pass along nint in the
defined panel function as did vref  - it comes in as missing, not 45.]

Hope this works for you.  I also placed the strip= into the call as I think
it looks nicer and am passing this along to you.

                > grp<-rep(1:10,each=100)
> mn<-(x-5)/10
> resp<-rnorm(1000,m,1)
> xx<-data.frame(resp,grp)
> xx$grp<-factor(xx$grp,levels=1:10,labels=paste("Group",1:10,sep=' '))
> m2<-sort(unique(mn))

> histogram( ~ resp|grp, data=xx,vref=m2,nint=45,xlab = 
        "Individual inbreeding coefficient", layout = c(5, 2), panel = 
        function(x, y, subscripts,vref)
                {
#                      print(subscripts)        
                panel.histogram(x, y)
                panel.abline(v = vref[max(subscripts)/46], lwd = 1, 
                        lty = 4, col = 6)
                },
        strip = function(...) strip.default(..., style = 1)
)

> histogram( ~ resp|grp, data=xx,vref=m2,nint=45,xlab = 
        "Individual inbreeding coefficient", layout = c(5, 2), panel = 
        function(x, y, subscripts,vref,nint=45)
                {
#                      print(subscripts)        
                panel.histogram(x, y)
                panel.abline(v = vref[max(subscripts)/(nint+1)], lwd = 1, 
                        lty = 4, col = 6)
                },
        strip = function(...) strip.default(..., style = 1)
)

The second alternative was provided by Michael Bramley (mbramley at att.net)
who suggested to superpose the histogram rather than the line, as folllows:

xyplot(~xx[,1]| xx[,2],panel=my.panel)
my.panel<-function(x,y) {
    hist(x,nclass=45,xlab="",ylab="")
    abline(v=const)
}

but this suggestion did not work out completely. 

Many thanks again to Jim Pratt and Michael Bramley for their assistance. 

Daniel Ruzzante

messages.subject: Re: [S] partial correlation(3)
messages.body_plain:
> Sorry I didn't specify the question clearly. I'd like
> to calculate the correlation between X and Y
> controlling the effect of (Z1,Z2,Z3...). I wrote some
> code to do this which is very slow. Splus must have
> something to calculate this efficiently. I just dont
> know where to find it. Thanks in advance. --Dan
> 
The following function does the job, but I don't know how fast it had 
to be...
cor.par <- function(x, which = (1:dim(x)[[2]])[ - partial], partial)
{
# x      ... data
# which  ...Indizes of interesting var.
# partial  ...Indizes of controlled var.
#
        if(is.data.frame(x)) x <- as.matrix(x)
        cor(lm(x[, which] ~ x[, partial])$residuals)
}

so with your data I do the following:

data <- cbind (X, Y, Z1, Z2, Z3)
cor.par(data, 1:2, 3:5)

I hope it does run!
Meinhard Ploner

messages.body_plain:
On Wed, 9 Aug 2000, alex kriezis wrote:

> I'm trying to source a file using source("filename")
> but I'm getting an error message. I'm using the 4.5
> windows version of S+ and I'm not quite sure under
> which directory should I place my file so that S+ will
> be able to source it. Any ideas?

I believe it is always the Windows working directory as specified in the
start-up directory in the shortcut you used to launch the program,
unless you set S_CWD or S_PROJ, in which case look them up in
the Programmer's Guide (although as I recall that has not always been
accurate).

You can also give an absolute pathname, with separator / or \\, 
for example

source("c:/bdr/MRI/testfile.q")

which will remove any possible uncertainty.

messages.subject: [S] Advanced/Specialized S-PLUS Courses (Aug & Nov)
messages.body_plain:
This email will give you details on the following specialized/advanced
courses offered by MathSoft, Inc during August and November, 2000:
1) S-PLUS for Statistical Data Analysis presented by Dr. Frank Harrell
2) Regression Modeling Strategies presented by Dr. Frank Harrell
3) Environmental Statistics Using S-PLUS presented by Steve Millard
_______________________________________________________________________
Course #1:  S-PLUS for Statistical Data Analysis presented by Dr. Frank
Harrell
View Full Course Description:
www.splus.mathsoft.com/splus/train/harrell_stat.htm
Course Description: This two-day course begins with a quick summary of the
S-PLUS language and objects and a comparison of S-PLUS and SAS. This is
followed by methods for inspecting, re-coding, re-shaping, and manipulating
data, some of which use extensions of S-PLUS found in the public domain
Hmisc library written by the instructor. Usage of S-PLUS for more advanced
statistical methods such as simulation and bootstrapping is surveyed. Then
basic sample size and power calculations are discussed, followed by an
example using the Hmisc library to simulate power for the Cox-logrank test
for comparing event times in a clinical trial in which drop-in, drop-out,
and delayed treatment response are present. Then major emphasis is given to
table making and S-PLUS and Hmisc graphical functions useful in everyday
exploratory work and to present final summary statistics. The course
concludes with discussion of some tools for making analyses reproducible, an
important facit for regulatory and other scientific review of final results.
Advantages of using S-PLUS in conjunction with the LATEX document processing
/ typesetting system for constructing reproducible statistical reports and
hyperlinked PDF documents are discussed.

Dates/City:     August 21-22    Chicago, IL

Price:          Commercial = $1050
                Government = $ 950
                Academic   = $ 950
                discount: Save $250 when you register for both Frank Harrell 
courses!
                Includes continental breakfast, p.m. snack, and course materials

Hours:          Days 1-2:  8:30am-5:00pm
                (Continental Breakfast: 8:00-8:30 daily)

For a more detailed course description, location information, and other
courses, please visit: www.splus.mathsoft.com/splus/train/2000schedule.htm

Register:       - Call Kim Kelly at: 800-569-0123 x278
                - Email: kkelly at splus.mathsoft.com
                - Web: www.splus.mathsoft.com/splus/train/train_registration.htm
_______________________________________________________________________

Course #2:  Regression Modeling Strategies presented by Dr. Frank Harrell
View Full Course Description:
www.splus.mathsoft.com/splus/train/harrell_regression.htm

Course Description: The first part of the course presents the following
elements of multivariable predictive modeling for a single response
variable: using regression splines to
relax linearity assumptions, perils of variable selection and overfitting,
where to spend degrees of freedom, shrinkage, imputation of missing data,
data reduction, and interaction surfaces. Then a default overall modeling
strategy will be described. This is followed by methods for graphically
understanding models (e.g., using nomograms) and using re-sampling to
estimate a model's likely performance on new data. Then the public domain
S-Plus Design library will be overviewed. Design facilitates most of the
steps of the modeling process. Next, statistical methods related to binary
and ordinal logistic and survival models will be covered. Four case studies
will be presented: an interactive exploration of the survival status of
Titanic passengers, a case study in data reduction and modeling of an
ordinal clinical diagnostic outcome, an interactive case study in developing
a survival time model for critically ill patients, and a case study in Cox
regression. In the hands-on computer lab, students will develop, validate,
and graphically describe multivariable regression models themselves.

                - Web: www.splus.mathsoft.com/splus/train/train_registration.htm

View Full Course Description:
http://www.splus.mathsoft.com/splus/train/environmental.htm

Course Description: This 3-day course covers basic and advanced concepts in
environmental statistical design and analysis, and shows how to apply these
concepts in practice using S-PLUS and the add-in module EnvironmentalStats
for S-PLUS. The course includes both lecture and hands-on instruction, with
each student using a PC to implement examples and exercises. Each student
will receive a set of course notes, which are based on the textbook
"Environmental Statistics with S-PLUS" that will be published by Chapman &
Hall/CRC Press in the fall of 2000.

Try the following:

  - click on Processes tab
  - find SPLUS.exe in the list of Image Names
  - right click on SPLUS.exe, choose Set Priority, then Low, then Yes

Splus should then run with CPU priority just above the null process.

  - Lane

messages.body_plain:
STATISTICIAN/BIOMETRICIAN

Position Description:

The Biometrics Research Department at Merck Research Laboratories, Merck &
Co., Inc. in Rahway, NJ is seeking a highly motivated
statistician/biometrician to work in its basic research and drug discovery
area.  Primary responsibilities include collaborating with scientists on
experimental design and data analyses, developing statistical and
exploratory data analysis software, developing new statistical methodology,
and co-authoring research presentations and publications.  

We collaborate with scientists in a wide range of disciplines, including
biology, biochemistry, microbiology, analytical chemistry, chemical
engineering, bioprocess development, genomics, bioinformatics, and
veterinary medicine, among others. Good oral and written communications
abilities are therefore essential, as is the desire to learn enough of the
relevant science to interact effectively.

A Ph.D. or equivalent in statistics (such as Masters with substantial
experience) or a related area is required. More specifically, we seek a
statistical scientist with strength in modern methods for the design and
analysis of complex studies and the analysis of large, complex, and often
"messy" data sets. Some of the specific statistical areas comprehended by
this description include data visualization, multivariate non-parametric
methods, pattern recognition, robust methods, Bayesian methods, nonlinear
mixed effect modeling, and chemometrics.  Equally important, we seek someone
able and eager to extend and broaden their statistical expertise to meet new
challenges. Ongoing education is an important part of the job. 

Good software skills are essential. Facility in S-PLUS is required.
Familiarity with other statistical and mathematical software (e.g. SAS(tm),
Matlab(tm), Mathematica(tm)) would be a plus, as would experience in any of
C, C++, Java, or SQL.

Prior experience in the pharmaceutical or related(diagnostic, chemical)
research would be helpful but is not essential. Formal education in
non-statistical areas like biology, chemistry, or computer science would

The selfish behaviour of S-PLUS 2000 with NT4 is indeed very selfish.
A collague carries out  also simulations (using the function nlminb)
and on some PC's go out of memory and on other PC's not !

Is this a wellknown problem? Are there some solutions?
My collague changed nlminb yesterday as advised in earlier emails
and the program runs now well.

But it is the obscure working of S-PLUS 2000 with Windows NT which
gives bad feelings!

Arnold

When I run a computationally intensive simulation on a 400 MHz NT4
machine with 256 Mb of memory, splus hogs all my resources, and if I try
to run other tasks, they run glacially slowly if at all.

Does anyone know of some way (via either splus or NT4 commands) that I can
limit
splus to using only about half of my memory and processor resources, so the
simulation can continue, but I can also get other things done?

I have been especially annoyed because I started a simulation in a
(similar) remote computer via PC-Anywhere, and now I can't even call
into that computer to check on progress because splus won't let the
modem answer.

Thanks for any help.

Dave

messages.body_plain:
>A collague carries out  also simulations (using the function nlminb)
>and on some PC's go out of memory and on other PC's not !

There are three ways (at least) of controlling memory usage in NT, and
leaving Splus to use as much as is available at the time.

- using the task manager options as observed early in this thread (quite
neat, but only active for as long as that application is in memory, I'd
guess). This is probably the best option.

- through the System properties (either on the context (right click) menu of
"My Computer, or via control panel/system) you can adjust the overall
performance of the system to favour background or foreground applications (I
think the default is foreground performance favoured). The foreground
application is the one with the active window.

- through the same control panel, you can bump up virtual memory. This
should reduce freezing etc. Make sure you set lots, preferably on a disk
which isn't used for your system, Splus program, or data. I use up to 1000MB
with a 500MHz, 256MB RAM machine.

Simon Kay

messages.subject_clean: SOLUTION RE: [S] Reducing splus 2000's selfish behavior with NT4
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to Brian Ripley, Siem Heisterkamp and Simon Kay for their quick and
usefull advices.
They showed us the way to find the essential point in the problem: WARNINGS in
function nlminb.
It seems that the warnings generated by nlminb are stored in memory.
Putting in Options / General Settings / Computations /Warnings Action in NO
WARNINGS
solved the problem.

Also changing the while-loops in nlminb was usefull, but not as good as putting
of the warnings.

Arnold Dekkers

> From: Sixten.Borg at astrazeneca.com

> NT.
>

> 
> > qqplot(sample1, sample2)
> > dev.print(postscript, file="figure1.ps")
> 
> Only, Microsoft Word can't seem to read a postscript file.

Usually it can, it just does not show a preview.  You can use
GSView (or epstool from the same source) to add a preview.  However,
this is only useful if you print on a postscript printer. Our students
do and use this all the time.  (As Word 2000 can be partially installed in
so many ways, you may need to add some bits.)

The most obvious solution is to use Export Graph on the File menu. That
allows all sorts of formats, and EMF can readily be imported into Word
(just don't edit it in Word or rotated text gets lost).  I believe
there is a command-line equivalent (but I'm on Unix here).

Some comments:

1) The postscript device on Windows does not produce encapsulated postscript,
and we have seen problems embedding its output in e.g. latex documents.

2) Export Graph allows export to postscript too, and that is 
encapsulated postscript.  At least on 4.5 we found that complicated
figures got corrupted, and used wmf2eps on EMF export.  Neither produce
so good a quality as postscript().

3) A third route is to use pdf.graph and convert that to PS via the
ExportPS addon to Acrobat.

4) Postscript can be converted to lots of other formats by GIMP, GSView,
ImageMagick and many other tools.  Almost all of these make a bitmap
and so lose quality, often drastically.

--

messages.body_plain:
Here is what you want to do, shown by an example:

   graphsheet(file="test.wmf",type="wmf")
   tsplpot(co2)
   dev.off()

Then start Word and use Insert > Picture > From File...  Specify the file
"test.wmf".  This gives maximum quality for Word, you see the picture on the
screen, and it prints well on any printer.

"wmf" stands for Windows Meta-Format and is the underlying format for
Windows programs graphics, as for Excel.  Although you can edit the picture
in Word, the results are usually unpleasant.

Another equivalent way that does not use an external file is just to plot
the graph in a window, select it, do Edit > Copy and then, in Word, do Edit
> Paste Special > and choose Picture (you can also paste as an S-plus
graphic object).

By using the graphsheet command (look up its arguments), you can specify
width and height etc.

  - Lane

messages.subject: [S] problem with using "offset" in poisson regression
messages.subject_clean: [S] problem with using "offset" in poisson regression
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am having a strange problem trying to use an offset variable in a poisson
regression (glm).  Here are the details:

I have a written a program in S-PLUS which runs the following glm call:

glm.obj <- glm(formula = C ~ X1 + X2 + X3 + X4 + X5 + X6 + X7, family =
poisson(link = log), data = SDF1, na.action = na.exclude, control =
list(epsilon = 0.0001, maxit= 50, trace = T))

FYI: I have replaced the variable names with basic names here for ease of
understanding.  'C' represents a count which is often 0 or 1.  I am using
S-PLUS 2000 for Windows NT 4.0.  There are approximately 10,000 records in
this data frame.

This poisson regression runs very quickly - in about 1-2 seconds max.  The
residual deviance value for this model is about 1000 on the average (I
actually run several poisson regressions in this program).

However, my actual response variable is a rate.  My understanding is that
when your response variable is a rate, and you determine that poisson
regression is appropriate, the denominator for the rate should be used as an
offset variable.  Therefore, given that C is my numerator, and D is my
denominator, I run the following glm:

glm.obj <- glm(formula = C ~ offset(D) + X1 + X2 + X3 + X4 + X5 + X6 + X7,
family = poisson(link = log), data = SDF1, na.action = na.exclude, control =
list(epsilon = 0.0001, maxit= 50, trace = T))

This is the same call as above, except I have introduced the term offset(D),
where D is the denominator for my rate (response variable).  The problem is
that the glm does not converge when offset(D) is in this glm call.  I
continually get this message:

Warning in glm.fitter(X[, "(Intercept)", drop = F], Y, w, offset = offset,
family: linear convergence not obtained in  50  iterations.

When I look at the trace of these runs, I see that the residual deviance by
iteration is extremely high (anywhere from 1+017 to 1+019, i.e., 10 to the
17th and 19th power respectively).  I doubt that changing the number of
iterations will have much effect, because the improvement in residual
deviance from iteration to iteration is quite small.

Could anyone shed some light as to why introducing offset(D) into the model
formula causes these problems?  I am not sure how to go about modeling this
data correctly without using an offset variable in poisson regression.  Does
anyone have an alternate way to analyze count data given that poisson
regression is appropriate?  Could I use the rate denominator in some other
way in the model function?

All help is appreciated!

Thanks,
Reid Gilliam
ORSA
GRCI, Inc.
rgilliam at grci.com

messages.subject_clean: Update: [S] problem with using "offset" in poisson regression
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to Brad Biggerstaff for helping me out on this one.  Using log(D)
instead of D as the offset variable seems to have solved my convergence
problem:

-----Original Message-----
From: Biggerstaff, Brad J. [mailto:bkb5 at cdc.gov] 
Sent: Thursday, August 10, 2000 12:00 PM
To: 'Gilliam, Reid'
Subject: RE: [S] problem with using "offset" in poisson regression

If D is your denominator, your offset should be offset(log(D)), as you're
using the log link.

With the rate, you're really modeling the mean of log(C/D) as a linear
funciton of your Xs.  So 

  log(C/D) ~ X*beta
is
  log(C) - log(D) ~ X*beta
is
  log(C) ~ log(D) + X*beta
is
  C ~ exp(log(D) + X*beta))

and there's where the log of the right-hand-side links the mean of the
linear predictor, log(D) + X*beta, to the mean of C, distributed Poisson.

brad

messages.subject: [S] [s] Summary: Leaps function, Which and Linear models
messages.subject_clean: [S] [s] Summary: Leaps function, Which and Linear models
messages.body_plain:
Hello,
a few days ago I sent a mail asking for help to automatize the writing of
the "formula" parameter in the lm() funtion. In particular, I wanted that
formula to be made up with the subset of independent variables pointed as
the "best model" according to the adjusted r2 (result given by the leaps()
funtion). At the end of this mail, I have pasted my original message.
Thanks very much to Samuel Buttrey sebuttre at nps.navy.mil (Samuel: I had to
add a "comma" to your expression "form"), Markus Loecher
loecher at scr.siemens.com and Frank E Harrell Jr fharrell at virginia.edu for
their useful help. I managed to do what I wanted following the indications
of Samuel and Markus. Frank advised me to bootstrap the process: it sounds
interesting and promising, I will also have at that. Thanks again to the
three of you.
Ana.

Follows the small script I made and the answers I got:
The script: 1-imports .txt tables from a directory to create dataframes,
2-runs the leap() function to find out the set of variables with the highest
adjusted r2, and 3- runs a linear model regression lm() with the previously
selected set of variables.

[s]-.-.-.-.-.-.-.-.
filenamestxt <- paste("d:\\ana\\pruebas\\sam", 1:10, ".txt", sep="")

outlist_ list(read.table(filenamestxt[1], header=T))
for (i in 2:10){
   outlist_ c(outlist, list(read.table(filenamestxt[i], header=T)))
   }

leap.names_ list(paste("lp", 1:10, sep=""))

for (i in 1:10){
   leap.names[[i]]_leaps(outlist[[i]][, 4:29], outlist[[i]][,3], int=T,
method="adjr2", keep=T, nbest=1)
   form_paste("formula=Y15 ~",
paste(unlist(unpaste(leap.names[[i]]$label[which((leap.names[[i]]$adjr2)==ma
x(leap.names[[i]]$adjr2))], ",")), collapse=" + "), ",",
"data=outlist[[",this.item,"]], na.action=na.omit")
  expression_paste("lm(", form, ")", sep="")
  leapnames[[i]]_eval(parse(text= expression))
  }
-.-.-.-.-.-.-.-.-
>  From Markus Loecher:
you could try to use
eval(parse(text = paste (....))) This evaluates strings as expressions.
So assuming you have a vector of variable names called LABELS (=
c("MEANCEREAL",  "MEANCATTLE", "APCTMODE", "DENSINUCL", "MUNEMPL24",.... ))
you would first get the index vector of the variables you want:
ind <- which((leap.names[[10]]$adjr2) = = max(leap.names[[10]]$adjr2))
Then you build your formula as a string in the following manner:
- Start with the first element:
FORMULA <- paste("Y15 ~ ", LABELS[
which(leap.names[[10]]$which[ind,])[1] ])
- Now add the remaining variables:
for ( i in which(leap.names[[10]]$which[ind,])[-1] ) FORMULA <-
paste(FORMULA, " + ", LABELS[i])
- After this your formula should be exactly the string you would like to
pass to lm !
I would use eval(parse(text = paste ("lm10_lm(formula = ", FORMULA, ", data
= outlist[[10]], na.action = na.omit)" )))

--.-.-.-.-.-
> From Samuel Buttrey:
Use unpaste() to break up the "label" component into pieces, separated where
the
commas are. This function returns a list, so call unlist() to get a vector.
Then paste() them back together with a plus sign in between the terms, and
finally call paste() once more to add the dependent variable on the left and
the other stuff on the right.

So this should work:

this.item <- 10
best.model <- 11

form <- paste ("Y15 ~ ", paste (unlist (unpaste
(leap.names[[this.item]]$label[best.model], ",")), collapse=" + "), "data =
out.list[[", this.item, "]], na.action=na.omit")

This gives a character string. You can either add "lm(" on the front and ")"
on the back to get a character string that you can execute as a command,
using eval (parse (text = <your character string>)), or enclose the formula
part with the formula() function and add the "data = " part later. Did that
make sense?

messages.subject: [S] Summary: Exporting a plot to Windows NT file.
messages.subject_clean: [S] Summary: Exporting a plot to Windows NT file.
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

Thank you for a number of good advice regarding my question how to export a
Splus graph into a file which Microsoft Word can read [Windows NT, Splus
2000]. I have tried to summarize the responses, and although I have not
tested all the proposed methods, I have included them all to make the
summary as complete as possible. Original question appended below.

Most of the advice recommended creating a WMF file (Windows Meta File),
which can be inserted into a Word document. The most straight-forward way is
to do the following [as suggested by Vladimir Piotrovskij (after just 16
minutes!), James Roger, Lane Bishop]

> graphsheet(format="WMF", file="figure1.wmf")
> plot() # create desired graphics
> dev.off()

In Word, use the menu Insert, Picture, From file...

Another way is to access the graph afterwards [as suggested by Leonid
Gibiansky].

> plot() # create desired graphics
> export.graph(Name = "GSD2", 
    ExportType = "WMF",
    FileName = "figure1.wmf")

In Word, do as described above. I can see that the export.graph() method has
it's merits in that it is something which can be done after running a script
that has not been prepared in advance to export its graphical output to a
WMF file.

Another way to do this [as suggested by Joseph F Lucke, Nick Locantore,
Brian Ripley] is to use the Splus menu File, Export graph, which offers a
large number of file formats including WMF. Although at a first glance, this
does not look like a script-based method, one can display the History window
(Splus menu Window, History, Display) to reveal that it actually uses
export.graph() to perform the action. The call to export.graph() can then be
used as described above.

John Fennick added more comments on the procedure in Word, which I would
like to add for the sake of completeness, although I have not yet examined
this:
> If you use the Insert/Object route in Word, you can easily 
> edit, with the S
> graphics editor, from the Word document as long as your 
> original graphsheet
> file is still available. S need not be open, double clicking 
> on the graph
> in the Word application will open it.
> 
> Procedure from Word is:
>       Insert/Object
> in the "Creat New" menu dialogue, select "SPlus Graphsheet", 
> this option
> should be there from the S installation.
> Then select tab
>       "Create from File"
> Browse to find your graphsheet file.
> Be sure to check the "link to file" box in the Create from 
> File dialog.
> and also check the "Float over text" box.
> 
> You can manipulate image location, size, shape, clipping, 
> etc. with the
> Format/Object menu in Word, or if you double click on the 
> image, you will
> be placed in the S graphsheet editor modifying the original S 
> file. Closing
> the editor when done will leave you in the S command sheet 
> and you must
> return to Word manually (not nice but hopefully you don't 
> need to do this
> often).
> 
> If you subsequently delete the original file, the image will 
> be retained in
> the Word file but you are then restricted to the very bad Word image
> editor, as Lane indicated.

Another response, from Peter Alspach, which I yet have not had the
oppurtunity to examine closer is as follows;
> I see you've had plenty of responses, but I figured I send 
> you a copy of the 
> little function I use:
> 
> p <- function(File="lpt2", Format="", Orientation="p", Sheet=2, ...)
> {
> #  To print to printer or file.  20 January 1999 (modified 1 
> November 1999)
> #  Allowable Formats are BMP, EPS, GIF, IMG, JPG, PCL, PCX, TIF, TGA  
> & WMF
> #  Only prints to default printer (ie HRN-Q_ADMIN) :-(
>   if(substring(File, 1, 3)=="lpt")
>   {
>     graphsheet(file=File, format='printer', orientation=Orientation)
>   }
>   else
>   {
>     graphsheet(format=Format, file=paste(base.dir, File, ".", 
> Format, sep=""),
>                orientation=Orientation)
>   }
>   dev.set(Sheet)
>   dev.copy(which=max(dev.list()))
>   dev.off(max(dev.list()))
> }
> 
> I work on a LAN with a number of printer options - the 
> default is trapped to 
> lpt2 (the colour is trapped to lpt3 but for some reason this 
> function won't print 
> to that ....)
> 
> Usage:
> 
> p() will print the graph of the current graphsheet (by 
> default Sheet=2)
> p('Figure1', 'WMF') will save the graph as a windows metafile 
> in a file called 
> Figure1.WMF (and analogously for the other formats).
> 
> Note the use of base.dir.  This is a character string I put 
> in every _data folder 
> so that when saving graphs and output it goes to the 
> appropriate folder.

Further comments on printer drivers which I also have not examined closer
are as follows;
> 1) The postscript device on Windows does not produce 
> encapsulated postscript,
> and we have seen problems embedding its output in e.g. latex 
> documents.
> 
> 2) Export Graph allows export to postscript too, and that is 
> encapsulated postscript.  At least on 4.5 we found that complicated
> figures got corrupted, and used wmf2eps on EMF export.  
> Neither produce
> so good a quality as postscript().
> 
> 3) A third route is to use pdf.graph and convert that to PS via the
> ExportPS addon to Acrobat.
> 
> 4) Postscript can be converted to lots of other formats by 
> GIMP, GSView,
> ImageMagick and many other tools.  Almost all of these make a bitmap
> and so lose quality, often drastically.

Kind regards,

Sixten Borg.

** ORIGINAL QUESTION.
** Dear Splus-users,
** 
** I am stuck with a problem that I imagine has a simple solution - but I
can't
** figure out how. I would like to save a graph into a file that can be
** accessed by Microsoft Word on Windows NT. I am using Splus 2000 on
Windows
** NT.
** 
** What I would like to do is something along the lines of...
** 
** > qqplot(sample1, sample2)
** > dev.print(postscript, file="figure1.ps")
** 
** Only, Microsoft Word can't seem to read a postscript file.
** 
** The actual format is not important, I simply want to create plots and
store
** in a document that can be accessed (in any possible way), and put into a
** word document. I would like to automate the process - otherwise it is
** certainly possible to cut and paste the plots.

=============================================
Sixten Borg
Statistician / Modeller
Health Economics & Outcomes Research
Clinical Science
AstraZeneca R&D Lund, S-221 87  Lund, Sweden

We have tried the wmf route many times and have consistently found

this won't work for Powerpoint for screen viewing.  But I'm
abandoning Powerpoint anyway because of a number of shortcomings.

messages.subject: [S] question on simple linear regression
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have the most naive and embarassing question on
statistics 101.

I'm trying to use some simple multiple linear
regressions to do some prediction work. I wonder when
doing prediction, does it matter if I include
multicolinear independent variables or
not-so-significant independent variables? By
not-so-significant, I mean the independent variables
which can not explain too much of the variance. The
reason is I dont really care much about the values of
beta themselves when doing prediction.

Can some one comment on this or point out some
papers/books I can read on this? I'd appreciate that.

Thanks so much.

Dan

messages.subject: Re: [S] question on simple linear regression
messages.body_plain:
Dan - for prediction, including collinear variables does not
hurt.  It actually hurts if you remove variables on the
basis of P-values because of biases in estimating the
residual variance and bias in remaining betas if you
remove variables.

See

@BOOK{mye90,
  author = {Myers, Raymond H.},
  year = 1990,
  title = {Classical and Modern Regression with Applications},
  publisher = {PWS-Kent},
  address = {Boston}
}

p. 379-381.

For problems with stepwise variable selection see
http://www.pitt.edu/~wpilib/statfaq.html
and
@ARTICLE{har96mul,
  author = {Harrell, Frank E. and Lee, Kerry L. and Mark, Daniel B.},
  year = 1996,
  title = {Multivariable prognostic models: {Issues} in developing
models,
          evaluating assumptions and adequacy, and measuring and
reducing
          errors},
  journal = Statistics in Medicine,
  volume = 15,
  pages = {361-387}
}

messages.subject: [S] question about deviance
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

There is probably a simple answer to this question, but I thought I would
ask it anyway.  Suppose I run a glm (poisson regression) using the
statement:

glm.obj <- glm(formula = Y ~ offset(log(D)) + X1 + X2 + X3 + X4 + X5 + X6 +
X7 - 1, family = poisson(link = log), data = SDF1, na.action = na.exclude,
control = list(epsilon = 0.0001, maxit= 50, trace = F))

Next, I use "anova" to produce the analysis of deviance table for the model
using these statements:

anovaoutput <- anova(glm.obj,test="Chi")
print(anovaoutput)

This is my anova output:

Analysis of Deviance Table  
Poisson model  
Response: Y  
Terms added sequentially (first to last)                  
        Df      Deviance        Resid. Df       Resid. Dev      Pr(Chi)

NULL                            10437           28175.3                    
X1      1       -125147.0       10436                   153322.4
0.0000000    
X2      1       121257.9        10435           32064.5         0.0000000   
X3      2       15791.5         10433           16273.0         0.0000000 
X4      1               0.3                     10432           16272.7
0.5907353 
X5      1       50.1                    10431           16222.5
0.0000000            
X6      7               5.8                     10424           16216.7
0.5612385          
X7      1       30.4                    10423           16186.3
0.0000000

My question is this:
What does it mean to have a negative deviance value for one of my
explanatory variables?  I thought deviance was similar in many cases to the
residual sum of squares which cannot be negative.  Does this mean there is a
problem with my model or does it imply something else?

Thanks in advance for your help!!
Reid Gilliam
GRCI, Inc.

messages.body_plain:
From: Florin Vaida <vaida at sdac.harvard.edu>
> This is the sequence of commands that raised my suspicions:
> 
> fisher.test( matrix(c(1,47,9,41), ncol=2) )     
>  #p-value = 0.0158      # Chisq p = 0.0233
> fisher.test( matrix(c(1,48,9,41), ncol=2) )
>  #p-value = 0.0157      # Chisq p = 0.0214
> fisher.test( matrix(c(1,49,9,41), ncol=2) )
>  #p-value = 0.0157      # Chisq p = 0.0196
> fisher.test( matrix(c(1,50,9,41), ncol=2) )
>  #p-value = 0.0079      # Chisq p = 0.0180
> fisher.test( matrix(c(1,51,9,41), ncol=2) )
>  #p-value = 0.0073      # Chisq p = 0.0166
> fisher.test( matrix(c(1,52,9,41), ncol=2) )
>  #p-value = 0.0069      # Chisq p = 0.0152

This is actually understandable from the way the 2-sided Fisher test is
defined (and IMHO, a good reason not to use the 2-sided test for data like
these).  The Fisher test in general reports the sum of probabilities of
all possible tables with the given marginals that are at least "as
extreme" as the observed table.  For a one-sided test on a 2X2 table,
this ordering is unambiguous.  The 2-sided test has to figure out how to
rank tables that are at the opposite extremes (i.e. the ones with (1,1)
cell "too big" or "too small").  The usual solution is to order the
tables by their probabilities under the null.

Now I haven't done the actual calculation but what I suspect is that in
Florin's first 3 tables, the observed table is slightly more probably
than another table in the opposite tail.  In the remaining tables, the
observed is slightly LESS probably than that table so it gets dropped out
of the sum, approximately halving the tail probability.  This is a
predictable consequence of the definition.

Now the philosophy.  (Anything about the Fisher test is almost certain to
generate a philosophical argument but at least this is not the usual one
about conditionality vs unconditionality.)  A two-sided test bases the
p-value for the alternative that is supported by the data (e.g. Y is too
big) on the sum of sizes for that alternative and another alternative
(e.g. Y is too small).  For an essentially symmetrical test like the
t-test where the difference betwen one- and two-sided is just doubling
the p-value, this is fairly innocuous.  In the 2X2 contingency table
case, the amount you add to the p-value for the possible tables in the
opposite tail varies in a complicated way, not directly related to the
p-value in the tail of interest.  I have trouble seeing how this makes
the test more informative.  If you are open a priori to both
alternatives, why not calculate the p-value for each (only one of which
will be interesting, at most) and then use that in your test (with a
Bonferroni correction if you want to control total size)?

So, David .... get that 1-sided test programmed for Version 5.2!

messages.subject: [S] Follow-up: Opinions on PowerPoint and editing graphics
messages.subject_clean: [S] Follow-up: Opinions on PowerPoint and editing graphics
messages.body_plain:
I've received several interesting communications since I made my
post earlier today about PowerPoint and wmf files.  Here are a
few more ramblings, to answer some of the questions I've been
getting.

1. Why abondon PowerPoint?

We recently gave a sponsor a large number of graphs to include in
a presentation.  The presentation turned out to be very unsatisfactory
for a variety of reasons, some of which could easily be fixed in
PowerPoint.  The sponsor used a silly distracting background.  Slide
titles could be read 100 yards away yet the "meat" of the slides
such as the graphs were made too small as per PowerPoint defaults.
Plots were distorted (see below) and so were tables we gave them
in Word format that they pasted into PowerPoint.  The sponsor had
trouble navigating slides quickly when questions arose.

I also find that composing PowerPoint slides takes more time
than using LaTeX, especially when inserting new elements and
moving bullet items at the bottom of one slide to the top
of another slide.  Equations are a real problem with PowerPoint.

Someone mentioned to me that one department in one of the
branches of the US military has forbidden PowerPoint from
being used, because of productivity loss and overuse of frills.

The biggest single problem with PowerPoint is that it offers
temptations to the composer to add non-substantive features
to the presentation.

2. What's a replacement?

PDF and Acrobat Reader or xdvi or ghostview, 
with slides composed using LaTeX
with seminar style or even using Word, no fancy backgrounds or
animation.  Navigation is simple, fast, and slides look scientific.
The latter is especially true using LaTeX - we use a style I
got from Jose Pinheiro - see LaTeX Examples entry near the bottom of
http://hesweb1.med.virginia.edu/biostat/s/EmacsTeX/

See http://hesweb1.med.virginia.edu/biostat/presentations/dilemmas.pdf
for an example of this format.

For those who like animation, there are new extensions to PDF
such as PPOWER4 (thanks to RE Darnell for pointing this out).

3. Is WMF hopeless?

I have not tested wmf created with the new wmf.graph function
in Splus 6.0 beta.

Usually all the editing that we need to do for imported wmf
files is re-sizing.  But just that will distort the graph,
especially if dotted or dashed lines are used, and in some
cases, if heavy lines are used.

4. Why edit graphs after production?

This is an excellent issue raised to me by Jim Pratt.  I actually
don't believe in it, for the reason Jim said - it gives other
folks the opportunity to change the "data content" of the graph.
Also, we commonly update graphs when new or corrected data arrive.
It's a time-waster to have to interactively edit the graphs
all over again.  Re-sizing graphs is another issue but still
problematic for wmf in our experience.

5. What format makes the most beautiful graphs?  postscript

6. Can inserted postscript graphs be viewed in PowerPoint?
Don MacQueen pointed out to me that you can open a ps file
in Adobe Illustrator and add a preview image to the file,
which PowerPoint will display own the screen.  File size
may increase.

Those of you who will be attending my 2-day course in Chicago
in 2 weeks will hear more about this, and about reproducible
research tools (see
http://hesweb1.med.virginia.edu/biostat/s/LiveDoc.html
for more about the latter).  

To me a general solution to many of the problems alluded to here
has LaTeX at its core.  LaTeX can produce different formats
from the same material (I'm finding that "if" statements are
invaluable in document procession), such as ps or pdf slides for
projection, hard copy reports, and on-screen pdf slides with
automatically-generated hyperlinks for navigating an electronic report.

I sure that every reader of s-news has opinions about all of these
areas, and I look forward to seeing them.
-- 
Frank E Harrell Jr              Prof. of Biostatistics & Statistics
Div. of Biostatistics & Epidem. Dept. of Health Evaluation Sciences
U. Virginia School of Medicine  http://hesweb1.med.virginia.edu/biostat
