messages.subject: RE: [S] fisher.test
messages.body_plain:
In resolution to my fisher.test() question:

1. fisher.test() works correctly, and as far as I can tell there is NO
bug in the algorithm or implementation.  I was wrong in suggesting there
might be one.

2. The discontinuity observed in the p-value has to do with the 2-sided
p-value dropping a "big" table in the opposite tail when passing
from (1/50,9/50) to (1/51,9/50).  This would happen, for example, every
time you move from (a/n, b/n) to (a/n+1, b/n). 
  Thanks to those pointing out this phenomenon, common to all discrete
tests.  Special thanks go to Alan Zaslavsky and John Mardo.

3. Most people won't care about this phenomenon, but since this can
make or break an interim analysis in a clinical trials, I do.  I suggest
instead  to multiply the 1-sided p-value of the extreme event (i.e., the
"small" p-value) by two.  StatXact, for example, currently offers that
option.  As Brian Ripley pointed out, the 1-sided p-value is available in
R.

Best,

        Florin

messages.body_plain:
I wish I could take time to add my frustrations to Frank's remarks,
especially as his note came in as I was struggling valiantly with PowerPoint
myself.  Maybe I will in fact make just a few observations.  Keep in mind
the context for me - production and constant revision by multiple authors of
a large number of modules for "Six Sigma" training at a corporation with
120,000 employees.  [I do some "research" type presentations too, and for
that usage, Frank's remarks would be much closer to on the mark.]

1.  The modules must be printable by a wide variety of people at several
large sites.  This means no embedded postscipt, as the majority of printers
can't handle it.

2.  Creation of graphs and putting them in PowerPoint has to be quick and
easy.  Intermediate processing by external programs is impossible, both for
time reasons (maybe a couple dozen graphs per module) and because future
revisors of the material may not have those extra programs.  Cutting and
pasting using the Windows clipboard from Minitab or Splus works quickly,
easily, and fairly well.  JMP is a pain.  Note that all resizing should be
done by holding down CTRL-Shift and dragging a corner to maintain the aspect
ratio, or by choosing Size on Format Object and clicking to maintain the
ratio.

3.  Mixtures of text and equations have to be done in Word and embedded in
PowerPoint.  Maintain aspect ratio here also when resizing.  Still rather a
pain - LaTex would be much easier, but I doubt if 5% of the module authors
have ever met LatTex.  Adding extra space: you have to double-click and drag
the sides or bottom of the object.  For all other editing, right-click and
choose "open" to edit the document in a separate Word window.

4.  All of our courses are given from computer projection, so we can switch
back and forth between PowerPoint and Minitab or Excel (the students all
have computers too, to follow and do exercises);  also who wants the weight
of a week's worth of transparencies to take on an airplane!  So projection
must be done from some program designed to show slides - powerPoint is much
better than Word, though maybe the Lotus or Corel programs might work as
well.

5.  We avoid the splashy junk stuff - animations, etc.  Keep it simple.

We get by, but I find PowerPoint one of the most frustrating programs I've
ever dealt with.  Of all the Office programs, this is the real dog.

  - Lane

messages.body_plain:
> The biggest single problem with PowerPoint is that it offers
> temptations to the composer to add non-substantive features
> to the presentation.

Related to this is one of my favorite quotes from Tufte's
\emph{The visual display of quantitative information}:

``Chartjunk does not achieve the goals of its propagators.  The
overwhelming fact of data graphics is that they stand or fall on
their content, gracefully displayed.  Graphics do not become
attractive and interesting through the addition of ornamental
hatching and false perspective to a few bars.  Chartjunk can turn
bores into disasters, but it can never rescue a thin data set.  The
best designs \ldots are \emph{intriguing and curiosity-provoking},
drawing the viewer into the wonder of the data, sometimes by
narrative power, sometimes by immense detail, and sometimes by
elegant presentation of simple but interesting data.  But no
information, no sense of discovery, no wonder, no substance is
generated by chartjunk. (Tufte, p.\ 121, 1983)''

I have observed a negative correlation between the amount of
non-substantive features in a presentation and the amount of actual
content in the presentations.  Presentations filled with
cart-wheeling bullet items, clip art, and superfluous 3D effects
tend to be light on content.  More often than not, non-substantive
features distract, rather than bolster, the points being made in a
speech.

Ed Malthouse

If I may add my very humble opinion on SPLUS to Powerpoint.  
The interface from SPLUS (PC) to 
Powerpoint is one of the main reasons I have avoided using
 the UNIX version of SPLUS.  I've found that a main reason to use SPLUS
graphics and interface to 
Powerpoint has been the fact that I don't have an army of programmers 
to design/tweak/tune/fiddle with graphics or general re-formatting of output
in SAS.  
I (have to) do all my graphics myself, including the cosmetic changes. 
I avoid re-editing graphics in Powerpoint.

Its far easier to explain a slide to a colleague over the telephone than to
explain statistical output. 

As has been noted the tricky part is  not to create "chartjunk". 
However, even with some chartjunk I've never been at a disadvantage by
actually showing data and statistical findings as a graphic.
I've been able to cut and paste slides from Powerpoint into WORD, although
that tends to create quite large WORD documents.

I promise that one of these days I'll learn LATEX, probably at the time I
decide to use my one month of acccumulated vacation. <grin>

messages.subject: RE: [S] scan (reading fixed format)
messages.body_plain:
When you use

scan("C:/temp/testfile.dat", what=list(NULL, 0), widths = c(2,3), 
flush=T)[[2]]     

you first get a list with two components, where the first one
just contains NULL (for the skipped columns) and the second 
contains the relevant data vector. The [[2]] selects the second 
component. 

If you need to read more variables, for instance one consisting 
of the three columns 101-103 and one in 151-153, you first skip
a 100, then read 3, skip 151-103-1 = 47 and then read 3.
If they are all character variables the code would be

temp <- scan("C:/temp/testfile.dat", what=list(NULL, "", NULL, ""), 
widths = c(100, 3, 47, 3), flush=T)     

This could then be made a data.frame by

data <- data.frame(temp)

or a matrix by, for instance,

data <- matrix(unlist(temp), ncol = 2)

(in both cases the NULLs disappear)

I've tried this on a dataset with 2500 4-character variables
and 6500 lines. It is SLOW but it works.

(However, if you have fewer columns but many more lines I would
recommend reading only one variable at the time since each
variable itself may be big and even putting them into a data.frame 
may be a problem).

Hope this helps.

Hakon

messages.subject: Re: [S] Storage Mode (fwd)
messages.body_plain:
I wrote to the list asking for help with the following error message:

Error in .Fortran("differ",: Cannot append - data would have length
greater than 0 (.Machine$integer.max/sizeof((token(72836268))))

Thanks to Bill Dunlap for explaining where it comes from; I pasted his
response below.  We ruled out the first possibility, and I'm going to look
into the second.

*  *  *  *  *

The error message comes from an internal C function
("check_data_overflow") that looks like it is being called with
incorrect arguments.  One reason for this may be that your differ
function calls this function (directly or indirectly).  Another
reason is that differ runs off the the end of some array (allocate,
say, 5 times as much space as you are for any arrays passed to differ to see
if that might be the case).

messages.subject: [S] lme non-nested random effects
messages.body_plain:
Gday

I'm trying to use lme (S+ 2000) to fit the following
model for 21 donors giving funds (y) in 4 different
years, using another continuous variable (x) as a
predictor:

y(it) = b0 + b1x(it) + e(it);
e(it) = error(i) + error (t) + error(it) (all Normal
iid rvs)

where subscript i (1:21) represents donor i and
subscript t (1996:1999) represents time t.  My data is
in the form of 84-element vectors consisting of y, x,
donor (a 21-vector of names repeated 4 times) and year
(a 4 vector of numbers each element repeated 21 times)

Q1 Is there something wrong with this model I have
missed?

Now, if I am prepared to make error(t) a fixed effect
rather than random the code is easy:

modA <- lme(y ~ x+as.factor(year),
random=list(~1|donor), method="ML")

But if I want error(t) to be random I am lost.  I try
the following code:

modB <- lme(y ~ x, random=list(~1|year,~1|donor),
method="ML")

Q2. The help file for lme seems to imply this will be
regarded as nesting donor under year, which is not
what I want (I think?).  How do I fit my model?

When I eventually get a model, I expect somewhere to
be able to find/deduce/extract a 21 element vector
residuals(i) and a 4 element vector residuals(t), as
well as a 84 element vector residuals(it).  But:

> dim(residuals(modB,0:2))
[1] 84  3

Q3. If I am on the right track, how do I find these
donor-level and year-level residuals from the above
84x3 matrix?  Alternatively, if I stick with modA, how
do I find the 21 element residual(i) vector I expect
from the 84x2 matrix?

grateful advice
PE

I have written a script to perform cross-correlation between two variables 
with missing data that may be applicable here.  The 'guts' are listed 
below:

ts.p<-rts(p)
ts.d<-rts(d)

for (i in 0:5)
{
        l.ts.p<-lag(ts.p,-i)
        test.data<-data.frame(ts.union(ts.d, l.ts.p))
        cr<-cor.test(test.data$l.ts.p, test.data$ts.d)
        rr<-round(cr$estimate,digits=4)
        ...
}

With minor modifications this should help with an acf with NA's.

messages.subject: [S] Answers to acf() and NAs
messages.body_plain:
All,

I got some good responses to my question on how to deal with NAs in
acf().  First, Erin Hodgess and John Maindonald suggested using is.na()
in the form

acf(x[!is.na(x)]

This forces acf() to ignore the NAs.  But, as John and my good friend
and fellow meteorologist Kim Elmore pointed out, while acf() will ignore
an NA and move on to the next point with a value, it will not increment
the lag.  This will result in erroneous values for each lagged
correlation, and is thus not acceptable.

Rick Dittmars provided the algorithm

ts.p<-rts(p)
ts.d<-rts(d)

for (i in 0:5)
{
        l.ts.p<-lag(ts.p,-i)
        test.data<-data.frame(ts.union(ts.d, l.ts.p))
        cr<-cor.test(test.data$l.ts.p, test.data$ts.d)
        rr<-round(cr$estimate,digits=4)
        ...
}

where p and d are univariate vectors.  It is a brute force
autocorrelation where the time series ts.p is lagged and the correletion
between it and ts.d is calculated.  The correlation functions have a
parameter that will cause rows containing NAs to be omitted from the
correlation calculation.  The loop determines the lag times to be
calculated, and I assume can be related to the second input variable for
acf().

messages.subject: [S] PAPER AVAILABLE on heteroscedasticity in multilevel modeling
messages.subject_clean: [S] PAPER AVAILABLE on heteroscedasticity in multilevel modeling
messages.body_plain:
Greetings, and apologies for cross-posting.

FYI, a paper on heteroscedasticity in multilevel/hierarchical modeling is
available for downloading in PostScript format from 

  http://www.bath.ac.uk/~masdd

(near the top of the page; the file is 404K in size and prints 21 pages).
The citation and abstract are as follows.

Browne WJ, Draper D, Goldstein H, Rasbash J (2000). Bayesian and likelihood
methods for fitting multilevel models with complex level-1 variation. 
Submitted.

                                 Abstract

In multilevel modeling it is common practice to assume constant variance at
level 1 across individuals. In this paper we consider situations where the
level-1 variance depends on predictor variables. We examine two cases using
a dataset from educational research; in the first case the variance at
level 1 of a test score depends on a continuous "intake score" predictor,
and in the second case the variance is assumed to differ according to
gender. We contrast two maximum-likelihood methods based on iterative
generalized least squares with two MCMC methods based on adaptive hybrid
versions of the Metropolis-Hastings (MH) algorithm, and we use two
simulation experiments to compare these four methods. We find that all four
approaches have good repeated-sampling behavior in the classes of models we
simulate. We conclude by contrasting raw- and log-scale formulations of the
level-1 variance function, and we find that adaptive MH sampling is
considerably more efficient than adaptive rejection sampling when the
heteroscedasticity is modeled polynomially on the log scale.

Comments on this paper would be welcome.

Best wishes, David Draper

messages.subject: [S] Summary: Error in stepAIC
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

in fact the error encountered when running stepAIC at the time I posted the
original message, attached at the end, turned out to be a printing error, as
pointed out by prof. Ripley.  I couldn't reproduce this error with the same or
other data sets.  But as I played with a similar data set I encountered a more
serious problem which generated several e-mail exchanges with prof. Ripley.
Here is a summary of the problem and the findings.

When running stepAIC, from the MASS library of Venable and Ripley, with the
following input arguments:

object    = Poisson NULL model(i.e. intercept only)
scope     = list(lower = "the NULL model", upper = "lots of variables")
scale     = irrelevent to this problem
direction = 'both'
k         = irrelevent to this problem

stepAIC was, rightly, doing a single iteration.  The lowest AIC being from the
NULL model.  Prof. Ripley spotted right away that the deviances were not correct
and hence the AIC's.  He asked me to make available to him the data set I was
working with and here is his conclusion:

> It's a bug in glm.  If you have weights and a null model then the
> weights are not recorded in the prior.weights component of the fit.
> Otherwise they are.  So stepAIC is doing unweighted fits.
>
> You can probably get around this by in addterm.glm and dropterm.glm
> replacing
>
>   wt <- object$prior.weights
>
> by
>
>    wt <- model.extract(m, "weights")
>
> Seems to work in your example, anyway.

To confirm his claim watch this:

> ttt.w.NULL <- glm(formula = fsinf ~ 1, family = poisson(link = log),
+                 data = vol05.all, weights = unsous)
> ttt.NULL <- glm(formula = fsinf ~ 1, family = poisson(link = log),
+                 data = vol05.all)

> attributes(ttt.w.NULL)$names
 [1] "coefficients"      "residuals"         "fitted.values"
 [4] "rank"              "assign"            "effects"
 [7] "df.residual"       "weights"           "y"
[10] "iter"              "family"            "linear.predictors"
[13] "deviance"          "null.deviance"     "R"
[16] "terms"             "formula"           "call"
[19] "control"

> attributes(ttt.NULL)$names
 [1] "coefficients"      "residuals"         "fitted.values"
 [4] "rank"              "assign"            "effects"
 [7] "df.residual"       "weights"           "y"
[10] "iter"              "family"            "linear.predictors"
[13] "deviance"          "null.deviance"     "R"
[16] "terms"             "formula"           "call"
[19] "control"

No prior.weights component gets recorded for either models.

> all.equal(fitted(ttt.NULL), fitted(ttt.w.NULL))
[1] "Mean relative difference: 0.1613021"

> all.equal(ttt.NULL$coef, ttt.w.NULL$coef)
[1] "Mean relative difference: 0.05669142"

although none of the two models have a "prior.weights" attribute their fitted
values differ, the coefficients differ also, hence the weights must be used some
how to fit the model BUT are not recorded as a component of the fit.
Accordingly stepwise functions; I am not claiming all of them, some may get the
prior weights from the call of the inputted object; fit unweighted models when
the input object is a NULL model with or without a weights argument.

I find this very disturbing.  To me it makes a lot of sense to start the process
of variable selection with the NULL model (so all one variable models will be
considered) when we have little information about relationships between
predictors and dependent and there is a large number of potential predictors.  I
am not claiming that models suggested by stepwise methods should be accepted
blindly, of course they should be scrutinized and be considered only as starting
points for deeper analysis.

probably would never have found the cause of the problem.

messages.subject: Re: [S] extracting what print methods "print"
messages.body_plain:
On Wed, 9 Aug 2000, O'Rourke, Keith wrote:

> 
> I would like to extract the medians that print.survfit calculates and prints
> from survfit objects... 
> 
> Is there something more elegant than creating a new function exactly like
> print.survfit but with "print" replaced by "return"?
> 
> Ths in adv
> 
> Keith O'Rourke
> Statistician, Department of Surgery and Clinical Epidemiology Unit
> University of Ottawa/ Ottawa Hospital
> 

I'm not sure it's more elegant, but 
motivated by the exact same need(!) I wrote a silly function
that picks up the printout and add it to the output value as
an attribute called "printout":

snatch <- function(x)
{
        tempfile <- tempfile()
        old.sink.level <- sink(tempfile)
        on.exit({
                sink(unsink.to = old.sink.level)
                unlink(tempfile)
        }
        )
        result <- eval(x)
        sink()
        fields <- count.fields(tempfile)
        printout <- split(scan(tempfile, what = list(""))[[1]],
rep(1:length(fields), fields))
        attr(result, "printout") <- printout
        result
}

If a function "func" prints stuff that you're
interested in,

result <- snatch(func())

should give the same as

result <- func()

but in addition attr(result, "printout") will be a list 
with one element for each line of printout, and each line 
separated into words as a character vector.

So in your case you could try 

result <- snatch(print(survfit(......)))

printout <- attr(result, "printout")
values <- as.numeric(printout[[3]]))
names(values) <- printout[[2]]

However, there may be better ways of doing it, and somehow I have
a feeling that if such a function was a Great & Useful thing to
have it would already have existed.........

Hakon

messages.subject: Summary RE: [S] extracting what print methods "print"
messages.subject_clean: Summary RE: [S] extracting what print methods "print"
messages.body_plain:
Obviously I owe a summary on this ... 

Generalities first;
1       I am not aware of why "print" is used in print methods rather than
"return"  (or return given as an option)
        (Although print methods are for "formatting only" its perhaps not
unexpected that some may do calculations in these print methods and "forget"
to provide these calculations elsewhere leaving them somewhat inaccessible )

2.      Not sure whether my suggestion of changing the "print" to "return"
in the print methods is more elegant than Gjessing's snatch routine  -  but
I like these two better than what some suggested of directly using the
functions inside the print methods that carry out the calculations because
doing that may over-ride options and defaults carefully implemented in the
print method (see specific note 2 below)

Specifics;

1. Terry Therneau pointed out it depends on the release

        Depending on your release---
        xx <- summary(survfit(Surv(.....
The matrix xx$table contains all the numbers printed out by print.survfit.
This was part of the summer 99 update of source code that I sent to StatSci.
I barely missed the 5.1 code, I suspect it is in Splus2000 but I don't run
on a PC so I can't be sure.
        Terry Therneau

2. With respect to individual survival curves from cox regression, when
there are strata rather than a single curve for a patient in their strata
you get curves for otherwise identical individuals in all strata and I am
not sure why one would want this. 

Hope this summary was not to sketchy.  
        (Ths to Prof Therneau, Harrell, McKinney, Ooi and Gjessing)

---------------

  xyplot(Mileage~Weight, data=fuel.frame, groups=Type,                          
        panel=panel.superpose)                                                  
                                                                                

Madeline Bauer:
----------------
Try the following (also see help file for panel.superpose)                      
{of course, everything depends on knowing the name of what you need!            
Who would have guessed "superpose"!!                                            
                                                                                
## test panel.superpose                                                         
                                                                                
## make some data                                                               
                                                                                
Y _ seq (1:20)                                                                  
X _ seq (101,120,1)                                                             
Z _ c(rep (1, 10), rep (2,10))                                                  
G1 _ c(rep (1, 5), rep (2,5))                                                   
G _ c( G1, G1)  

# plot with "standard" trellis superpose.symbol settings                        
                                                                                
xyplot(Y ~ X | Z, data=dat,                                                     
     groups=as.character(G),                                                    
     panel=function(x,y, ... ){                                                 
     panel.superpose (x,y, cex=0.75 , ... )}                                    
     )                                                                          
                                                                       
# change superpose.symbol settings                                              
sps _ trellis.par.get ("superpose.symbol")                                      
sps                                                                             
sps$pch[1:2] _ c(1,16)                                                          
trellis.par.set ("superpose.symbol",sps)                                        
                                                                                
xyplot(Y ~ X | Z, data=dat,                                                     
     groups=as.character(G),                                                    
     panel=function(x,y, ... ){                                                 
     panel.superpose (x,y, cex=0.75 , ... )}     

rm (dat)   

James Pratt:
----------
If I understand you correctly, I think you are trying to duplicate what         
panel.superpose was written for.  Look at the panel.superpose function
code

Patrick Connolly

messages.body_plain:
All,

I received this email from X. Ju (aka The Trashpicker,
trashpicker at hotmail.com) regarding my recent posting about not being
able to use NAs in acf().  It is an interesting way of filling missing
data. 
 

> Reading thru recent posting on S+ list and noticed your 
> question about NAs
> 
> I find that for my purposes, and maybe yours, there is wide range of 
> usefulness for a 'preprocessor' to turn raw vectors of 
> timeseries info (or, 
> via 'apply', matrices of) into vectors of 'last known non-NA 
> value'.  Then 
> input this vector to 'acf' or many other functions
> 
> 
> NAfix_function(x){
> x_c(-1,x)
> while (any(is.na(x)))
> x[is.na(x)]_x[(1:length(x))[is.na(x)]-1]
> x[x==-1]_NA
> x_x[-1]
> x
> }
> 
> >NAvec <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, NA, NA, 5, NA, 6, NA, NA, NA, 7, 8, 9, NA, 10)
> >NAvec
> [1]  1  2  3  4 NA NA  5 NA  6 NA NA NA  7  8  9 NA 10
> >NAfix(NAvec)
> [1]  1  2  3  4  4  4  5  5  6  6  6  6  7  8  9  9 10

In my quest for finding a way around the NA problem, I came across a
function called na.gam.replace() that will replace NAs with the mean of
all the non-missing values.  Unfortunately, that is not appropriate for
what I'm doing.  A mean or linear or cubic spline fit using the end
points surrounding the missing data values is what I need.  I could not
find a function that specifically does that.  Does anyone know of any?
Thanks much.

The S-PLUS team is looking for beta testers for S-PLUS 6 for Solaris and
Linux.  We'd love to get your feedback on the new features in S-PLUS 6,
particularly:

        * Java-based Graphical User Interface, and Java connectivity
        * Multiple Imputation library for analysis of data with missing values
        * New robust statistics library

The sooner we get feedback the more time we have to make changes for the
final release, so if you're in a position to install and test immediately
(and if your organisation is typical, that means not reliant on an IT
department :) ) you'd make an ideal tester.

To be able to beta test, you will need:

        * Access to the Internet (to access the Beta Program website)
        * A current S-PLUS for Unix/Linux licence, and experience in
          using and (ideally) installing S-PLUS
        * A SPARC-32 workstation running Sun Solaris 2.6, 2.7 or 2.8
                OR
          An INTEL PC running Linux kernel 2.2.5 or higher, with glibc 2.1.2,
                libc6 and f2c.lib (Red Hat 6.1 satisfies these requirements)
        * At least 64Mb physical RAM
        * Around 150Mb of free disk space
        * Time and patience to install and test S-PLUS 6

If you'd like to participate in the beta test program, please email
betazone at splus.mathsoft.com with your name, organization and area of

messages.subject: [S] data (evaluation) frame problem - HELP!!!!
messages.body_plain:
S-plus gurus:

I am totally confounded by the S+ "feature" of data (evaluation) frames.
Maybe someone can help me understand how to get around the problem.

I have a function called "fit4gammas" that creates a mixture of 4 gammas.
I want to bootstrap this function to look at the distribution of the calculated
mixture proportions for about 75 different patient datasets. To do this I
wrote this simple function called "boot.comets".

(Actually the function had a lot more going on with it but I reduced it to
bare minimum until I get this problem resolved.)

Using SPlus v 4.5

"boot.comets" <- function(cometdat, B=1000){

  print(paste("Starting boot.comets function where: B=", B));

  print(paste("Using input Dataset for patient", 
as.matrix(cometdat[1,"Patient"]),

    " ID", as.matrix(cometdat[1,"PatNum"])));

  temp.mixture <- bootstrap(cometdat,
    fit4gammas(cometdat, debug="F", show="F", iter=50), B=B,
    group=cometdat$Time, save.indices=T, assign.frame1=T);

  plot.resamp(temp.mixture);

  temp.mixture;
}

# call routine to bootstrap patient 61;
p061.boots <- boot.comets(p061)

# look at bootstrap summary stats;
summary.bootstrap(p061.boots);

This call to summary.bootstrap give the following error:

Error: Object "cometdat" not found
Dumped

The problem is obviously with the $Call object in the bootstrap list, where

p061.boots[["call"]]:

bootstrap(data = cometdat, statistic = fit4gammas(cometdat, debug = "F", 
show = "F", iter

	 = 50), B = B, group = cometdat$Time, assign.frame1 = T, save.indices = T)

Obviously, "cometdat" was a function parameter that was needed
to pass the input data frame to the bootstrap function....it resides only in
the evaluation frame for "boot.comets".

If I were working in a language like "C" this would not be a problem....
....haven't got a clue how to get around this S+ "feature"

What to do.....????
Any help would be appreciated.

Yes, I did read V&R and the SPlus Programmer's guide, but...still stuck.

messages.subject: [S] NAfix <- function(x)
messages.body_plain:
NAfix <- function(x,subst=-Inf){
#  propagate last known non-NA value
#  if x starts with a series of NA's, replace by subst
  spec <- max(x[!is.na(x)])+1
  x <- c(spec,x)
  while (any(is.na(x))) x[is.na(x)] <- x[(1:length(x))[is.na(x)]-1]
  x[x==spec] <- subst
  x <- x[-1]
  x
}
 
NAvec <- c(NA, NA, 1, 2, 3, 4, NA, NA, 5, NA, 6, NA, NA, NA, 7, 8, 9, NA, 10)
NAvec
# [1] NA NA  1  2  3  4 NA NA  5 NA  6 NA NA NA  7  8  9 NA 10
NAfix(NAvec)
# [1] -Inf -Inf    1    2    3    4    4    4    5    5    6    6    6    6    7
#[16]    8    9    9   10
NAfix(NAvec,0)
# [1]  0  0  1  2  3  4  4  4  5  5  6  6  6  6  7  8  9  9 10

messages.subject: [S] Fighting About the Justice for Medical Practice in Korea
messages.subject_clean: [S] Fighting About the Justice for Medical Practice in Korea
messages.body_plain:
Fighting About the Justice for Medical Practice in Korea

   The Ministry of Health and Welfare, Republic of Korea and Blue House 
(Presidential Office) have been wrangling for the past two years over the 
Medical Reform in which new regulations call for physicians can only 
prescribe and pharmacists can only dispense medications for outpatients 
starting past July 1st this year.  It sounds very civilized as similar 
systems have been practiced in most developed countries for years.  Up 
until this point, the physicians have been allowed to prescribe and 
dispense medications for the sake of their patients' economic interests and 
at the same time, pharmacists have also been allowed to dispense/sell drugs 
without physicians' prescriptions for patients' convenience. As Korea has 
made a significant stride in industrializing herself in 1970s, the 
government started to provide nationwide quasi-governmental health 
insurance system beginning late 1970s.  The system is an essentially co-  
payment system for which all workers have been deducted for premium from 
their paychecks.  The employer and government also pay for their share of 
premium.  The current regime made a campaign promise as they come into the 
power to pay 50% of health insurance premium from the government budget and 
yet so far the government has taken only 25%.  Due to improper management 
by the government, the health insurance fund is rapidly diminishing and its 
status is at brink of bankruptcy.  To the eyes of government and public 
alike, physicians are regarded as rich and affluent class in the society. 
 So that they put lid on the healthcare reimbursement fee schedule to 
control the inflation of cost of living in the country.  The average cost 
of living in Korea today is pretty much the same as that in the US. 
 Nation's physicians are greedy, right?  That may be so.  But not-so-  
pleasing a few counter-examples for physicians can be shown as follows: 
approximately US$3.10 for outpatient examination fee and US$3.15 for 
prescription fee of 14days medication.
   In order to relieve from the economic burden of national health 
insurance system, the President Kim Dae Jung proposed  a strange remedy of 
medical reform.  They curtail physicians' right of dispensing medication, 
however, leaves pharmacists to sell certain drugs without physicians' 
prescription, for example.  The patients, who purchase drugs without 
physicians' prescription, have to pay for on their own.  On the other hand, 
patients may be encouraged to stop by drug stores directly by making the 
whole prescribe-dispense system very cumbersome.  In doing so, government 
can save insurance funds.
   Therefore, practicing physicians, residents, interns, medical students 
and medical faculty members are up in arms nationwide against the 
irrelevant and infeasible medical reforms.  The bottom line is that 
physicians' pride is hurt. Their practices are currently limited to 
inpatients care, emergency care and emergency surgeries until government 
can come up with acceptable modifications of new regulations.   For some 
unknown reason, this democratic government is losing its cool to this 
professional group, they used anti riot police force to disrupt a peaceful 
demonstration within the ground of Yonsei University in Seoul on August 12, 
2000 which resulted in some injuries.
   The medical education here is a uniform 6-year curriculum after high 
school.  After that rotating internship, residency for specialty and 
fellowship for furthering specialized fields are the same as that in the 
US.  The Korean government does not subsidize any education or medical 
training that operate under the capitalistic principle.  However, the 
health insurance program is operating under the socialistic system.  When 
it comes to medico-legal litigation, it now operates under capitalistic 
system again.  This confusion is the cause for concern and source of 
conflict today in Korean society.

The following is an excerpt of statement issued by the Policy Development 
Subcommittee, one of the leading medical school, Faculty of Kyungpook 
National University School of Medicine, Taegu, Korea on the current 
outpatient crisis which typifies the atmosphere created by unprepared 
governmental officials' forceful implementation of a new regulation:
   We as the member of the Policy Development Subcommittee of Outpatient 
Crisis Management Faculty Team, Kyungpook National University School of 
Medicine would like to issue regrettably the forth coming statement.
- Our loving students, colleagues and trusted patients and their family 
members, we are forced to abandon our noble duty as the professor for our 
loving students and mentor of our bright residents since we are no longer 
able to convince you to keep our mission and duty as taught by the great 
Hippocrates;
- We are deeply saddened by the fact that we have to leave our many 
agonizing outpatients unattended;
- We are not going to ask for sympathy from officials or so-called health 
policy experts who are lacking realism for them not thinking of what's good 
for many ailing patients;
- We dare ask you the Minister of Health and Welfare, why do you insist 
that this crippled medical reform must be proceeded even if you admitted 
just recently that the whole system is ill-prepared so that it will cost 
patients a great deal of more money, pain and inconveniences;
- We dare ask you Mr. President, do you really know what you have done with 
current university education reform and medical reform in which you insist 
unprecedented financial self-sufficiency of such institutions, however, it 
deceives the public;
- Parents of medical students, Intellectuals, and Koreans, we do not trust 
this government of dishonesty since it gives deaf ears on truth which is 
worse than previous autocratic military regimes and even our kings of 
ancient feudalistic kingdom;
- Good friends of Non Governmental Organizations, we would like to ask you 
to come and observe what's really going on in medical education and 
teaching hospitals today with which we hope you will open your eyes toward 
real world;
- Please Mr. President, we hope you regain your usual sense of realism and 
logical approach; importing physicians from the Philippines or simply 
increasing reimbursement is not the answer for this crisis; and finally
- Dear our students, please do not blame slow but sympathetic professors, 
we will try to do our best to safeguard safer and better practice of 
medicine in this country.

Aug. 15. 2000

Bupwan Kim, M.D., Ph.D.
Department of Budget Planning, Kyungpook National University Hospital
Bupwkim at knu.ac.kr

messages.body_plain:
All

I received only one response to my query on the above but it was from Jose'
Pinheiro and definitive in its scope and helpfulness.  For the information
of the list, please see below for Jose's advice - many thanks.

cheers
PE

Peter Ellis
Curtin University

-----Original Message-----
From: Jose Pinheiro [mailto:jcp at research.bell-labs.com]

Dear Peter,

> I'm trying to use lme (S+ 2000) to fit the following model for 21
> donors giving funds (y) in 4 different years, using another
> continuous variable (x) as a predictor:
>
> y(it) = b0 + b1x(it) + e(it);
> e(it) = error(i) + error (t) + error(it) (all Normal
> iid rvs)
>
> where subscript i (1:21) represents donor i and
> subscript t (1996:1999) represents time t.  My data is
> in the form of 84-element vectors consisting of y, x,
> donor (a 21-vector of names repeated 4 times) and year
> (a 4 vector of numbers each element repeated 21 times)
>
> Q1 Is there something wrong with this model I have
> missed?

Your model looks fine and can be fit using lme. The random effects
have a crossed structure in this case, so it requires some tweaking of
lme call in order to fit it. I show one way that it can be done down
below.

> . . .
>
> But if I want error(t) to be random I am lost.  I try
> the following code:
>
> modB <- lme(y ~ x, random=list(~1|year,~1|donor),
> method="ML")
>
> Q2. The help file for lme seems to imply this will be
> regarded as nesting donor under year, which is not
> what I want (I think?).  How do I fit my model?

Well, you will probably get an error message if you try to use this
model specification. You can fit the model with the crossed random
effects using the pdBlocked and pdIdent classes:

  > modB <- lme(y~x,
  +   random = pdBlocked(list(pdIdent(~year-1), pdIdent(~donor-1))))

By default, lme will assume that all observations belong to a common
group and the pdBlocked/pdIdent specification will create independent
random effects for each year and for each donor, with the year random
effects having the same variance and similarly for the donor random
effects (thought the year variance will be different than the donor
variance).

> When I eventually get a model, I expect somewhere to
> be able to find/deduce/extract a 21 element vector
> residuals(i) and a 4 element vector residuals(t), as
> well as a 84 element vector residuals(it).  But:
>
> > dim(residuals(modB,0:2))
> [1] 84  3
>
> Q3. If I am on the right track, how do I find these
> donor-level and year-level residuals from the above
> 84x3 matrix?  Alternatively, if I stick with modA, how
> do I find the 21 element residual(i) vector I expect
> from the 84x2 matrix?

The donor and year random effects need to be extracted with ranef()
function, not resid(). The e(it) residuals are extracted with
resid(mod.B) (these are the raw residuals). ranef(mod.B) will produce
a one row matrix (a single group is assumed) with 25 columns. 21 of
them will correspond to donor and 4 to year -- the column names will
make it clear which are the ones you want.

There is an example on how to fit lme models with crossed random

messages.subject: [S] partial regression plots vs. partial residual plots
messages.subject_clean: [S] partial regression plots vs. partial residual plots
messages.body_plain:
I am having difficulty understanding what S-Plus uses for its partial
regression plots in the GUI-generated regression diagnostics. I think I
have it fiugred out, but I would like to check it with someone.

I am used to partial regression plots (a.k.a. added variable plots,
adjusted variable plots; Neter et al.1996, Applied linear statistical
models).
These are defined for a model Y = X1 + X2, where the plot of the
marginal effect of X1  is a plot of
e(Y|X2) vs. e(X1|X2).

***I am comfortable in saying that these added variable plots show the
relation between the response and X1 that is not explained by X2.

I am aware that,

"A partial residual plot is a plot of r i + b k x ik
versus x ik where r i is the ordinary residual for the i-th
observation, x ik is the ith observation of the kth predictor and
b k is the regression coefficient estimate for the kth predictor."
(S_PLUS User guide)

The partial residual plot seems similar to the added variable plot,
EXPECT that the x -axis (X1) includes variation that is correlated with
X2, whereas the added variable plot X axis removes the covariation
between X1 and X2.

***It seems to me that the partial residual plot also shows the relation
between X1 (in original units) and the variation in the response that is
not explained by X2.

But ... I am leaving something out, something I don't fully comprehend.
Would anyone care edit my simple summaries (indicated by ***) so that
they capture the subtle differences between these two plots?

Many Many thanks in advance,
Henry

> Error in lmList: Argument "cluster" is missing, with no default:
> lmList(Orthodont)
> Dumped
> 
> page 11: > Ortho.fit1 <- lme(fixed = distance ~ age, data = Orthodont,
> + random = ~ age | Subject)
> Error in lme.formula: Argument "cluster" is missing, with no default:
> lme.formula(fixed = distance ~ age, data
> = Orthodont, random =  ~ age | Subject)
> Dumped
> 
> I tried many ways to get around this problem, unfortunately with no
> success at all. It seems to me it has something to to with the "argument
> cluster".
> 
> I would be very grateful for any kind of advice.

Your problem is due to version skew.  You are using NLME 3.x model
specifications with the 2.1 version of the library.

The lme/nlme functions available with S-PLUS 3.x and S-PLUS 4.x are
from version 2 of the NLME library.  Version 3 of the library,
released in 1997, changed the names of arguments and some of the model
specification.  We realize that this is inconvenient but we did it
because the new form has several advantages relative to the old form.
In particular, the new version allows specification and fitting of
models with nested random effects.

NLME 3.3, the latest version for S-PLUS, is available at
                      http://nlme.stat.wisc.edu/
for S-PLUS 3.x for Unix, S-PLUS 4.x and 2000 for Windows, and S-PLUS
5.x for Unix or Linux.  We would recommend that you install this new
versions. 

The recent book "Mixed-Effects Models in S and S-PLUS" (Springer,
2000) that Jose Pinheiro and I wrote describes the use of the NLME 3
library in detail.

messages.subject: RE: [S] adding mean and median indicators to scatter plot
messages.subject_clean: [S] adding mean and median indicators to scatter plot
messages.body_plain:
This can be achieved fairly easily with the user-defined smoothing option of
the scatterplot.  The following example connects the means of groups of
points (grouped by the X variable) by lines; it could be modified fairly
easily so that the user-defined smooth is the median in the locality of each
X and NA elsewhere.

1. Copy the function summary.smooth to a script window in S-PLUS, and run it
(use the menu: Script | Run)

2. Open the your data file

3. Control-click to select columns x, y

4. Open the 2-D plot pallette, and select "Loess" (2nd button on 4th row)

5. Right-click on a data point, and choose Smooth/Sort...

6. For Smoothing Type, select "User"

7. For Function Name, enter "summary.smooth" (without the quotes)

8. Click OK

You should now have a scatter plot, with lines drawn through the means at
each time point (x).  You can calculate any statistic you like; for example,
repeat steps 5-7 above but enter "fun=median" (without quotes) in the Other
Arguments box to draw lines through the median.

summary.smooth <- function(x, y, z, w, subscripts=NULL,
        panel.num, fun=mean)
{
        if(!is.null(subscripts)) x <- x[subscripts]
        if(!is.null(subscripts)) y <- y[subscripts]
        miss <- is.na(x) | is.na(y)
        x <- x[!miss]
        y <- y[!miss]
        stats <- tapply(y,x,fun)
        x.out <- as.numeric(names(stats))
        y.out <- stats
        idx <- sort.list(x.out)
        list(x=x.out[idx], y=y.out[idx])
}

--

I've found the user-defined smoothing feature to be a bit stubborn and hard
to use: you can update the definition of the user-defined smoother all you
want, but the plot never gets updated until you change the smoothing option
to use some other smoother, re-draw the graph, and then change it back to
your user-defined smoother.  That, and being sufficiently aphasic that I can
never recall the damned calling sequence, has led me to use an alternative
approach that I find easier:

1. Create a data frame with the x and y values you want to plot, using the
same names for the column labels as you used in the original plot (makes
axis labels work);
2. Selecting the plot window you want to add the smooth to;
3. Shift-selecting the plot method to add the smooth to the plot.

Adding conditioning variables to the new data frame allows conditioning
plots to go through unscathed.

Of course, although I find this easier, you mileage may vary.

messages.body_plain:
A few days ago I posted a query regarding (vertical) boxplots with boxes of
differing colors.  I had responses from Don MacQueen and Anona Thorpe and
used their suggestions to cobble together a simple function presented below.
It satisfies my requirements with regard to short term needs, but could also
benefit a great deal from some error checking, added functionality,etc.  For
those with an interest, feel free to improve upon it.  For those who
requested a copy of any contributed functions consider the function below a
starting point.

Peter Scherer
Dow AgroSciences

# simple function to create boxplots with boxes of differing colors
# 22 Aug 2000

# sample data
y.dat <- rnorm(500)
x.dat <- rep(1:10,rep(50,10))
boxplot(split(y.dat,x.dat))

# function to create boxplot with a col vector
col.boxplot <- function(response,group,col=2:(length(unique(group))+1)){
        y.range <- range(response)

messages.subject: [S] Functions for higher moments, plus handy memory saving mean function
messages.subject_clean: [S] Functions for higher moments, plus handy memory saving mean function
messages.body_plain:
I offer some functions I wrote for my own use to calculate skewness and
kurtosis. They automatically omit NAs, though you could put in a "na.rm"
parameter like the mean function if needed.

Also I have included a set of functions for calculating means and variances
on the fly. They can be useful, for example, in simulations when you are
accumulating the results one by one on a number of different variables, as
it conveniently packages all the basic summary statistics in a single
object, and avoids the need for maintaining very large vectors.

For example, if you are doing 1 million simulation runs, and tracking 10
variables, you will need to maintain around 20 MB for 10 objects, and then
calculate them at the end. If you crash, you lose the lot. Using these
functions you keep a running tab on the mean, var, etc, using <1 KB for all
10 objects. Calling mean.accum() for every simulation run is not efficient,
but you can always store, say, 1000 runs, and then pass them through
mean.accum(). I have found that they completely eliminate memory problems
for large simulations, and often increase the speed.

They could be adapted easily to do the skewness and kurtosis, or the moments
of any order, or any analogous statistic. NAs need to be removed before
calling mean.accum().

"skew" <- function(x)
{
        x <- na.omit(x)
        meanx <- mean(x)
        varx <- var(x)
        skewx <- (sum((x - meanx)^3))/(varx)^1.5/length(x)
        return(skewx)
}

"kurt" <- function(x)
{
        x <- na.omit(x)
        meanx <- mean(x)
        varx <- var(x)
        kurtx <- (sum((x - meanx)^4))/(varx)^2/length(x
                )
        return(kurtx)
}

"mean.make" <- function()
{
#       cat("Used for on the fly calculation of mean and stdev\n")
#       cat("mean.make sets up list variable\n")
#       cat("mean.accum adds vector values to list variable\n")
#       cat("mean.var .stdev .cv calculate statistics from list\n")
#       cat("max and min can be accessed directly from the list\n")
        return(list(n = 0, min = Inf, max =  - Inf, sum = 0, sumsq = 0))
}

"mean.accum" <- function(average, x = 0, do.max = T, do.min = T)
{
        n <- length(x)
        average$n <- average$n + n
        average$sum <- average$sum + sum(x)
        average$sumsq <- average$sumsq + sum(x^2)
        if(do.max)
                average$max <- max(average$max, x)
        if(do.min)
                average$min <- min(average$min, x)
        return(average)
}

"mean.mean" <- function(average)
{
        return(average$sum/average$n)
}

"mean.cv" <- function(average)
{
        return(mean.stdev(average)/mean.mean(average))
}

"mean.stdev" <- function(average)
{
        return(sqrt(mean.var(average)))
}

"mean.var" <- function(average)
{
        return(average$sumsq/average$n - (average$sum/
                average$n)^2)
}

USAGE EXAMPLE:
# Set up mean variable
mean.temp_mean.make()
# Start accumulating samples of a normal distribution
for(i in 1:1000){
        x_rnorm(100)
        mean.temp_mean.accum(mean.temp,x)
}
# Print results
print(mean.temp)
print(mean.var(mean.temp))

GIVES OUTPUT

> print(mean.temp)
$n:
[1] 100000

$min:
[1] -4.317897

$max:
[1] 3.984291

$sum:
[1] 363.4966

$sumsq:
[1] 100107.8

> print(mean.var(mean.temp))
[1] 1.001064

skewness <- function(x)

messages.body_plain:
Sure.  Let S be the covariance matrix of the individual measurements

Then

alpha.cronbach<-
function(S)
{
 d <- dim(S)[1]
 (d/(d - 1)) * (1 - sum(diag(S))/sum(S))
}

This function is not bullet-proof against invalid arguments for S (S a
scalar for example).

             arr[qx, qy, 1, drop=c(F,F,T)]

Even if qx or qy reduces to one element, I still want to get a 2-dimensional
array back.  Here's a function I wrote that does this, with syntax
             .slice(arr, qx, qy, 1, drop=c(F,F,T))
Notice that a single value for "drop" gets recycled to length(dim(arr)), so it
behaves just like the current "[" function.

.slice <- function(a, ..., drop=T, use.names=T) {
  b <- a[..., drop=F]                   # Drop dimensions selectively
  drop <- drop & dim(b)==1              # Recycles "drop" if necessary
  dn <- dimnames(b)
  dimnames(b) <- NULL
  if (sum(!drop) < 2) {                 # Create a vector (or scalar)
    dim(b) <- NULL
    if (use.names) names(b) <- unlist(dn[!drop])
  } else {                              # Create an array
    dim(b) <- dim(b)[!drop]
    if (use.names) dimnames(b) <- dn[!drop]
  }
  b
}

   Can I make ".slice" (perhaps renamed "[.array") a method for "["?

                -- David Brahm, Fidelity Investments (brahm at alum.mit.edu)

variables for fitting models.  Does anyone have experience running SPLUS

messages.subject: RE: [S] SPLUS performance on large datasets?
messages.body_plain:
The answer, as with most questions of this nature, is "it depends".

Mainly, it depends on your how much virtual memory (swap space) and physical
RAM you have.  As long as the operating system will provide as much virtual
memory as S-PLUS requires, the analysis will finish ... eventually.
However, if S-PLUS is required to use a lot vitual memory during the
computation, you can expect things to run much slower than if only physical
RAM were used.  Unix is generally pretty good at this; Windows 95 and
Windows 98 perform poorly when virtual memory is in use;  Windows NT and
Windows 2000 are somewhat more efficient.

For this reason, we recommend S-PLUS users have physical RAM at least 5
times the size of the data, to allow room for temporary computations during
the analysis.  This is a very rough rule of thumb though: simple analyses
like regression and analysis of variance do not require much in the way of
temporary computation, but other analysis (eg logistic regression) can
require up to 50 times the data size for working data.

In all but the most trivial cases the more physical memory you have, the
faster S-PLUS will run when analysing a large database.

For example, I created an S-PLUS data object (data frame) with 100,000
observations: a continuous response and 100 categorical variables each with
3 categories: about the size you were discussing.  I used the following
S-PLUS code:

v1 <- rnorm(nrow, 1, 0.3)
testdat <- data.frame(y=v1)
for(i in 1:ncol) {
  cat(i)
  nextv <- list(as.factor(sample(letters[1:3], nrow, replace=T)))
 names(nextv) <- paste("v",i, sep="")
 testdat <- cbind(testdat,nextv) }

This data object is about 42 Mb in size:

> object.size(testdat)
[1] 41812499

I then performed a linear regression using all 50 variables as predictors
using the following code:

> options(object.size=Inf)
> obj <- lm(y~., data=testdat)

The first line turns off the inbuilt safety-limits on object sizes to allow
S-PLUS to analyse such a large database.  The second line fits the linear
model, which has 201 parameters.  Using a development build of S-PLUS 6
under Linux with 256Mb of RAM and 600Mb of swap, this took about 16 minutes.
At its peak, the S-PLUS process was using about 300Mb of virtual memory
(combined RAM and swap).

So if it's linear modelling you're interested in, you're looking at several
minutes for a problem of the size you mention, on a Unix machine with
sufficient physical RAM.  For more complicated problems (logistic
regression), it could take even longer, but then this is a very
computationally intensive problem and without changing your modelling
strategy (e.g. sampling data) the machine's just gotta crunch the numbers,
and that takes time.

Incidentally, a point of nomenclature: "StatServer" is a product in the
S-PLUS range that serves such analyses over the Web.  It only runs on
Windows though, so I'm not sure if this is what you were referring to below.

# David Smith

messages.subject: Re: [S] statistics question
messages.body_plain:
E. Balali asks:

> I had a question. I will be glad if you answer it:
> 
> For testing collinearity of independent variables in linear regression
> analysis, can we do a linear regression analysis within the
> independent variables?  In the sense that independent variables one by
> one be dependent for anothers. Can we infer that the entered variable
> in equation in this manner has a collinearity with dependent variable
> (that is really independent but here as dependent)? Thanks.  I wait
> for your answer.

There are a couple of points here.  Collinearity of independent
variables in a linear regression, given the model matrix, is a
mathematical property which you can measure, (in several ways, but
still, an objective, discernable property), not a statistical property
for which you can test and make inferences upon (other than in a
trivial sense).  (With the way your question is phrased I'm not sure
if you were making that distinction.)

Having said all that, the answer to your question is probably "yes",
in the sense that the computations that go into the collinearity
diagnostics are precisely the same as those that go into regression.
In fact the usual collinearity measures are just measures of the
degree to which any one x-variable can be predicted linearly from all
the others in the usual regression sense.  In my view this is a start,
but it is not the only way collinearity may be appreciated since it is
a property of several variables in combination, not of each variable
in isolation, but that's a longer story...  

If you wanted to investigate collinearity in a specific case by doing
regression calculations using selected independent variables as
dependent variables, I'd encourage you to go ahead and see what you
can discover.  Basically I think your intuition is correct.

--

messages.subject_clean: [S] Use of xlab() in trellis graphics: summary
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to Stephen Smith, Vicki Lancaster, Jim Pratt, Patrick Connolly
and Madeline Bauer for their answers.

My original post:

> in trellis graphics (like xyplot()), often the
> labels on the y-axis are too close
> to the labels. This is because by default
> the numbers are plotted horizontally,
> not parallel to the axis like in plot().
>
> Using plot(), I would use 
>
> mtext(side=2,"text",line=5)
> 
> to put the labels farther away from the axis.
>
> I can adjust the text size, font and color
> in xyplot() by using 
>
> xlab=list(text="text",cex=1.2, ...)
>
> but the use of for example 
>
> xlab=list(text="text",cex=1.2,line=5)
>                               ^^^^^^
> gives me the error message
>
> Error in mtext: Invalid argument name: line
>
> That's strange: mtext() is used to place the labels,
> but it does not recognize arguments common to it. I
> guess they don't get passed through correctly.

All but one suggested to use mtext() after calling the trellis
function. This works fine, if you define xlab("") within
trellis.

Jim Pratt however found a "trellis only" solution, using the page= argument:

JP> One work around I have used is to pass xlab (or ylab)  blank text string
with a
JP> large cex value to make enough space for my desired label.  Then use
mtext within
JP> the page option to actually place the label.
JP> 
JP> For example, I have a plot where the y-axis label is jumbled with y-tick
labels. 
JP> So within the xyplot function, I use the following code:
JP> 
JP> 
JP>   xyplot(resp~covar|group,data=my.df,
JP>    xlab='Size (um)',ylab=list(' ',cex=1.5),ylim=c(0,1e6),
JP>     page=function(x)
JP>             mtext('Concentration
(counts/mL)',side=2,line=par("oma")[2]-1,outer=T))
JP> 
JP>             With this use, setting cex=1.5 in ylab list and passing a
blank string
JP> basically provides space for the label.  Increase cex value to add more
space.  
JP> Then use mtext within page to place the y-label on every page.
JP> I had written this after S-Plus tech support could not come up with a
solution.

I checked it out and this very elegant solution works fine !

Thanks to all of you !

Greetings

Marcel
Marcel.Baumgartner at rdls.nestle.com

Hi everybody,

I am using the 3.4 version of S+ for Unix and have some C-functions  
calls embedded in S+ routines (memory allocation is done via 'S_alloc').

Several crashes occur (outside C, in S+) which cause 
a) the function called to terminate and with the next simple S+ command S+
   to produce a bus error or
b) S+ to terminate or
c) S+ and x-emacs to terminate.

What they have in common is that S+ seems to allocate waste amounts of
memory and complains about not having enough dynamic memory. The weird
thing is that everything works fine using the entire data set (1370 x 14).
Only if I am using a subsample these problems occur (with the exact same
settings and parameters as before, which means the same loops have to be 
gone through). 
The first subsample used was defined by certain values of one covariate,
then I tried random samples and the problem persisted. No complicated
statistical or mathematical operations are done in S+ (matrix inversion,
model fitting, etc.) and no missing values are contained in the data set.

These are some of the things I already tried:
- Set memory.size to Infinity
- Extract the subsample outside the function call 
- Convert the functions to S+ 5.1
- Run everything outside x-emacs
- Check if the data was read correctly
- ...

and nothing helped. 
Has anybody ever encountered similar problems? I would be very grateful
for any comments on this.

Thanks,

messages.subject: RE: [S] SPLUS performance on large datasets?
messages.body_plain:
One things that always amazes me in discussions of
large datasets, is the implicit assumption that the
program's answer will be correct.  The possibility
that cumulated rounding error may completely 
swamp the calculated coefficients is never considered.

I have one example (not on S-PLUS) with approximately
300,000 observations and 8 variables, for which I know
the correct answer to ten digits.  The packages on
which I have run this problem deliver 3-5 digits of
accuracy.

Of interest: how to tell when the problem exhausts the
limits of 32-bit word double precision (assuming a PC)
and the particular method of solution (Cholesky will
crap out before QR, but QR is a memory hog)?  Any
suggestions?  I have searched the literature, to no
avail.

Please reply to me.  I will summarize for the list.

thanks,

Bruce

messages.body_plain:
Many replies were received on my question regarding the execution of a
simple anova.. Thanks for all helping, and not flaming the 'novice'. Special
thanks also to Vince Matassa, who personally phoned me to help, and Bill
Venables, who had a look at my data and checked my results were correct.

    Paul Kristiansen wrote:-

I'll let the gurus confirm your approach, it seems ok to me (I'm 1 step
above novice).  I don't think you HAVE to have rep in your formula, but
perhaps you can try it with and without, keep your eye on the Residual MS in
the anova table, lower is better?

One thing is to check the diagnostic plots to check the assumptions of AOV.
You could start with:

my.aov_aov(%CleanCane~rep+BilletLength*FanSpeed, data=my.data.frame)

Then test assumptions ...
* variance not dependant size of fitted values, use:
plot(fitted(my.aov), resid(my.aov))

.>* normality, use:
>qqnorm(resid(my.aov))
>qqline(resid(my.aov))  # optional, this just puts a line through the points
>to make assessment 'easier'

>If the points in the resid vs. fitted plot are dispersed unevenly, and/or
if
>the qqnorm plot has the 'tails' moving away from a straight line, you may
>need to transform the response variable (e.g. %CleanCane), using e.g.
>sqrt(y), log(y), 1/y to rerun the lm, then re-plot the diagnostics to see
if
>it is better, etc.  As a new chum, I find the interpretation of diagnostic
>plots a bit subjective.  That's OK if you are experienced and can evaluate
>the nuances and act appropriately. Nevertheless, it is important to at
least
>look at those plots.

>There is some discussion about this on pp.161-167 in Venables and Ripley
>book Modern Applied Statistics with S-Plus, 3rd edition. They uggest using
>studres (need to load library(MASS) first) rather than the regular resid,
>especially for qqnorm plots.

>Once you are happy with the assumptions, you can run the aov, get your aov
>table
>summary(my.aov)
>and then refer to the tables of means and std errors to look at what's
going
>on
>model.tables(my.aov, type="means", se=T)

>Give interaction.plot() a go too, e.g.
>interaction.plot(BilletLength, FanSpeed, %CleanCane, data=my.data.frame)

Bill Venables added:-

> Hi,
>
> I work with sugar cane in Far North Queensland, and I am trying my
> best to conduct an analysis on a trial I ran recently.. in short it is
> a 3 rep 2*2 factorial (2 billet lengths, 2 fan speeds) in which I am
> assessing harvesters on their ability to clean cane. Each experimental
> unit is a rake of three ten tonne bins...
>
> my data frame consists of a billet length column (containing long or
> short), a fan speed column (containing fast and slow) and a rep column
> (containing 1,2 or 3), all designated as factors. The subsequent
> columns include productivity data, such as % clean cane..
>
> 1. I am analysing this with analysis of variance.. is this the best
> thing? I think so as the experiment is balanced.

>>You have designed it as an analysis of variance experiment, so an
>>analysis of variance seems like it might be the natural place to start
>>with the analysis, at least!  You may have to look at whether or not
>>you need a transformation, of course.  Percentage data can be very
>>non-normal, particularly if the values are all near one end of the
>>percentage range.

> 2. the formula I use is (for example) :-
> %CleanCane~rep+BilletLength*FanSpeed
>
> Is my layout correct, and is my formula right?

>>It looks OK, but you are going to be in some difficulty if you use
>>names that start with "%" (or use it anywhere for that matter).  This
>>isn't genstat (thank goodness)!

Bill then also personally had a look at my data and helped me with the
analysis. It turned out that what I was doing was pretty much right - but
thanks for your help Bill.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------

> Hi,
> I'm not sure about the tables you're referring to, but I know of two
> confidence intervals useful in small samples. The first inverts the
> standard hypothesis test for p, putting the true p in the denominator,
> rather than \hat p. Tom Santner called intervals of this type
> "q-intervals". Here is S+ code for the q-interval for a binomial:
>
> qintbinom <- function(x,n,alpha=.05){
> #
> # Routine to construct q-interval for binomial sample with x successes
> # in n trials. Default is alpha=.05, or a 95% confidence level.
> #
>   z <- qnorm(1-alpha/2)
>   phat <- x/n
>   center <- phat*n/(n+z*z)+(z*z/(n+z*z))*.5
>   adj <- sqrt(phat*(1-phat)/n*(n*n*z*z/(n+z*z)^2)+((z^4)/(n+z*z)^2)/4)
>   plow <- center-adj
>   phigh <- center+adj
>   list(plow=plow,phigh=phigh)}
>
>
> The other possibility is an exact interval based on the true binomial
> probability function. There is no unambiguous way to define the two tails
> in this problem, but the standard method is the Clopper-Pearson interval.
> StatXact gives the Sterne/Blyth/Casella interval, which is shorter. Here
> is code for the Clopper-Pearson interval:
>
> exactbinomci <- function(x,n,alpha=.05,tol = .Machine$double.eps^.25){
> #
> # Routine to construct the exact Clopper-Pearson confidence interval
> # for a binomial sample with x successes in n trials. Default is
> # alpha=.05, or a 95% confidence level.
> #
>   if (x==0) plow <- 0 else {
>     flow <- function(p,x,n,alpha){pbinom(x-1,n,p)-1+alpha/2}
>     plow <- uniroot(flow,c(0,x/n),x=x,n=n,alpha=alpha,tol=tol)$root}
>   if (x==n) phigh <- 1 else {
>     fhigh <- function(p,x,n,alpha){pbinom(x,n,p)-alpha/2}
>     phigh <- uniroot(fhigh,c(x/n,1),x=x,n=n,alpha=alpha,tol=tol)$root}
>   list(plow=plow,phigh=phigh)}
>
> As you can see, this solves equations for p; the tolerance controls the
> precision of that solution.
>
>
> I hope these help.
>
>       Best,
>
>       Jeff

> Here is my own crude little newton's method search.  Use at your
> own risk :-)
>
> albyn
>
> "binom.CI"<-
> function(x, n, level = 0.95, eps = 0.00001, max.iter = 100)
> {
>         a <- (1 - level)/2
>         # find upper endpoint of CI
>         if(x == n) P.max <- 1
>         else
>         {
>         OP <- (x+.5)/(n+1)
>         P0 <- OP + 1.8 * sqrt(OP * (1 - OP))/sqrt(n)
>         P1 <- OP + 1.9 * sqrt(OP * (1 - OP))/sqrt(n)
>         if(P0 >= 1)
>                 P0 <- 0.98
>         if(P1 >= 1)
>                 P1 <- (P0 + 1)/2
>         done <- 0
>         iter <- 0
>            while(!done) {
>                 Y0 <- pbinom(x, n, P0)
>                 Y1 <- pbinom(x, n, P1)
>                 slope <- (Y1 - Y0)/(P1 - P0)
>                 step <- (a - Y0)/slope
>                 P <- P1
>                 P1 <- P0 + step
>                 if(P1 >= 1)
>                         P1 <- 0.99999000000000005
>                 if(P1 <= 0)
>                         P1 <- 9.9999999999999995e-07
>                 P0 <- P
>                 if(abs(P0 - P1)/P1 < eps)
>                         done <- 1
>                 iter <- iter + 1
>                 if(iter > max.iter)
>                         {
>                         done <- 1
>                         cat("P.max failed to converge after", iter,
>                                 "iterations\n")
>                         }
>            }
>            P.max <- P1
>         }
>         # find lower endpoint of CI
>         if(x == 0) P.min <- 0
>         else
>           {
>         OP <- (x+.5)/(n+1)
>         P0 <- OP - 1.8 * sqrt(OP * (1 - OP))/sqrt(n)
>         P1 <- OP - 1.9 * sqrt(OP * (1 - OP))/sqrt(n)
>         if(P0 < 0)
>                 P0 <- 0.050000000000000003
>         if(P1 < 0)
>                 P1 <- P0/2
>         done <- 0
>         iter <- 0
>
>         while(!done)
>                 {
>                 Y0 <- 1 - pbinom(x - 1, n, P0)
>                 Y1 <- 1 - pbinom(x - 1, n, P1)
>                 slope <- (Y1 - Y0)/(P1 - P0)
>                 step <- (a - Y0)/slope
>                 P <- P1
>                 P1 <- P0 + step
>                 if(P1 <= 0)
>                         P1 <- 9.9999999999999995e-07
>                 if(P1 >= 1)
>                         P1 <- 0.99999000000000005
>                 P0 <- P
>                 if(abs(P0 - P1)/P1 < eps)
>                         done <- 1
>                 iter <- iter + 1
>                 if(iter > max.iter) {
>                         done <- 1
>                         cat("P.max failed to converge after", iter,
>                                 "iterations\n")
>                 }
>                 }
>           P.min <- P1
>           }
>         c(P.min, P.max)
> }

messages.body_plain:
if I might make an observation on S-Plus and this list;

I am a recent adopter of S-Plus and trying to learn to use it well; I am 
also a user of Stata, and there are several features of Stata and it's 
community of users that might help those of us who are new to S-Plus 
(probably veteran users  as well).

1. Stata, through its "webseek" feature, allows searching for help topics 
not only in addons, but across linked directories to help files, FAQ, and 
archives of user written code at various locations on the net.  This is a 
tremendous boon, as there are lots of user developed modules that 
tremendously extend the utility of the base program; such enhanced 
searching capability would be a nice addition to S-Plus.

2. The Stata newslist "statalist" is very active, and individuals generally 
always respond to the list rather than to individuals, and the original 
message is copied in the text.  While many of the S-news responses are 
eventually compiled and forwarded to the list, it appears that a great many 
are either never answered or are not eventually forwarded.  I find that 
both the dynamic exchanges and often discussions are interesting and 
helpful, and wish S-news responses occurred more on the list rather than as 
private dialogues.

It seems to me that both of these features must help reduce the need for 
tech support involvement, and would therefore be worthwhile.

Thanks for the opportunity to raise these issues, and thanks to those on 
this list who take the time to answer questions posed on the list, and to 
those who compile and forward their responses.

messages.body_plain:
I hope that MathSoft takes a serious look at the Webseek
capability of Stata.  I think it's a great idea.

Related to finding functions such as binconf that are in MathSoft-
distributed libraries written by users, these functions can be
easy to find but you must know which library to search if
you haven't already activated the library with library( ) or
File ... Load library ...

One particular note about binconf: it will compute the "exact"
beta-F-confidence interval (no iterations required for this)
or the more accurate Wilson confidence interval.  Note that
as Agresti et al discuss in their American Statistician article
on binomial confidence intervals, the price of exactness is
conservatism.

messages.subject: [S] The nsmall argument to format().
messages.body_plain:
I have just noticed that if you apply format() to a matrix which has
some NA entries, ***and*** if you give a value to the nsmall
argument, the result loses its matrix nature.

E.g.:

 > mmm <- matrix(1:9/100,3,3)
 > mmm[3,3] <- NA
 > format(mmm)
       [,1]   [,2]   [,3] 
[1,] "0.01" "0.04" "0.07"
[2,] "0.02" "0.05" "0.08"
[3,] "0.03" "0.06" "  NA"
 > format(mmm,nsmall=3)
[1] "0.010" "0.020" "0.030" "0.040" "0.050" "0.060" "0.070" "0.080" "NA"

This occurs both in Splus 3.4 and 5.1 for Unix (running under Solaris 2.7).

Is this a bug?  Is it a known bug?  Is there a known fix?

                                        cheers,

                                                Rolf Turner
                                                rolf at math.unb.ca

messages.body_plain:
At 14:47 26/08/00 -0300, Rolf Turner wrote:
>
>
>I have just noticed that if you apply format() to a matrix which has
>some NA entries, ***and*** if you give a value to the nsmall
>argument, the result loses its matrix nature.
>
>E.g.:
>
> > mmm <- matrix(1:9/100,3,3)
> > mmm[3,3] <- NA
> > format(mmm)
>       [,1]   [,2]   [,3] 
>[1,] "0.01" "0.04" "0.07"
>[2,] "0.02" "0.05" "0.08"
>[3,] "0.03" "0.06" "  NA"
> > format(mmm,nsmall=3)
>[1] "0.010" "0.020" "0.030" "0.040" "0.050" "0.060" "0.070" "0.080" "NA"
>
>This occurs both in Splus 3.4 and 5.1 for Unix (running under Solaris 2.7).
>
>Is this a bug?  Is it a known bug?  

Actually this seems to be one of the least consistent parts of the whole
system.  The general question seems to be "which attributes of an argument
does a function return in the result?"  It's not just that a general
convention is hard to formulate and promulgate, it's that some very
well-known functions behave very inconsistently in this respect.  For
example if X is a matrix, why is it that sqrt(X) is a matrix with the same
structue, but pnorm(X) is a vector?

This has been annoying me for some time so I am pleased for an excuse to
get it off my chest... :-)

> Is there a known fix?

There's always a fix, Rolf.  It just may not be what you wanted.

mmm0 <- mmm
mmm0[] <- format(mmm, nsmall = 3)

or, if you want a deliberately obscure one-liner:

mmm0 <- do.call("structure", c(list(format(mmm, nsmall = 3)),
attributes(mmm)))

(more seriously, this might give you a clue on how to write a suitable
local replacement for format() that does what you want.)

Bill Venables.

messages.subject: Re: [S] Programming challenge
messages.body_plain:
At 15:48 25/08/00 -0400, Winfred Lambert wrote:
>
>I've been asked to resend this message with more detailed information -
>I hope this is better: 
>
>SPLUS 2000, Windows 2000
>
>Here's a programming challenge.  I have 10 dataframes with columns
>containing 5 categories: 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5.  Each dataframe represents a
>meteorological reporting station.  I am computing the correlations
>between the categorical data for 2 stations at a time.  Whenever there
>is a 5 in one dataset AND a 5 in the other dataset at the same time, I
>do not want that pair to be considered in the correlation calculation.

This is still hard to see just what is going on.  Why would you hold the
data from each station in a separate data frame?  (Are we using "data
frame" in the same sense?  I wonder.)  To make any headway with the problem
we have to assume that each data frame has the same number of rows and that
the rows of separate data frames correspond, is that what you mean?  You
should say so.  

More seriously, why would you want to exclude points on the basis that
*both* are 5's?  Frankly a statistician would say it looks very suspicious,
but I am not wearing that particular hat at the moment...

>How do I tell cor() to ignore such a pair?  Thanks.

Well, you can't of course, not directly at any rate.  You have to get rid
of them yourself first.  Here is an obvious, lazy way of doing it with
absolutely no bulletproofing...  

You can't get away without some sort of loop as far as I can see so I will
assume your data frames have names S1, S2, ..., S10 and that in each case
the first component is the one that enters the correlation calculation (or
else you must provide some other way of accessing them inside a loop).

R <- diag(10)
for(i in 1:9) {
        x <- get(paste("S", i, sep=""))[[1]]
        for(j in (i+1):10) {
                y <- get(paste("S", j, sep=""))[[1]]
                keep <- !(x == 5 & y == 5)
                R[j,i] <- R[i,j] <- cor(x[keep], y[keep])
        }
}

You should be warned that with such irregular deletion patterns there is no
guarantee the resulting correlation matrix makes all that much sense.  It
may not even be positive definite, for example.

Bill Venables.

>(probably veteran users  as well).

>2. The Stata newslist "statalist" is very active, and individuals generally 
>always respond to the list rather than to individuals, and the original 
>message is copied in the text.  While many of the S-news responses are 
>eventually compiled and forwarded to the list, it appears that a great many 
>are either never answered or are not eventually forwarded.  I find that 
>both the dynamic exchanges and often discussions are interesting and 
>helpful, and wish S-news responses occurred more on the list rather than as 
>private dialogues.

Although I often "go public" myself (though not as often as I "go private"
these days) I feel obliged to offer a word of caution about this idea.
S-news used to be small enough (and slow enough) for this policy to be
manageable, but if everyone replied publicly these days traffic would
become a real issue.  I think that while the list is not monitored and
controlled (and what a hideous, full-time job that would be) the practical
protocol has to be to encourage people to respond privately as much as
possible and for the questioner to reply to the list with a summary.  (Says
he, just having broken that rule 10 minutes ago with a reply to Winifred
Lambert's problem!)
In a sense I would like to see the old free-for-all once again, too, as I
know how to sift through email pretty quickly (I have to!), but the effect
of heavy traffic is often to alienate those users who most need the help
and advice that the list offers and they just switch off, which is a real
pity.

>It seems to me that both of these features must help reduce the need for 
>tech support involvement, and would therefore be worthwhile.

Well, I suppose that anything that encourages users towards a deeper
understanding of the system and the subject will reduce the need for tech
support, but I would not hold up such a reduction as a primary reason for
the list.  I would see it as more for sharing ideas, experiences and code
and for generally fostering a  sense of (albeit virtual) community based on
shared experiences.  Unlike most other lists, the developer/vendor keeps a
low profile on this one and it is run by the users themselves.  While the
MathSoft folks do not often say very much they are listening, so it also
provides a way for users collectively to speak to the vendor about the
direction in which they would like the system to develop.  (Well, at least
in principle...  Are you there, David?)

Bill Venables.
