messages.subject: [S] ISIPTA '01: Preliminary Call for Papers
messages.body_plain:
Your help with circulating this announcement locally would be very much
appreciated. We apologise if you receive multiple copies of this
message.

If you didn't receive this mail through an electronic mailing list, this
means that you have expressed some interest in the previous ISIPTA
symposium, or that we received your address from one of our colleagues
who thought this message might be of interest to you.

If you do not want to receive further information about ISIPTA '01,
please send a short message saying so to smc at decsai.ugr.es.

++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++

ISIPTA '01

THE SECOND INTERNATIONAL SYMPOSIUM ON
IMPRECISE PROBABILITIES AND THEIR APPLICATIONS

Cornell University
Ithaca, NY, USA
26 - 29 June 2001

PRELIMINARY CALL FOR PAPERS

++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++

Encouraged by the success of the First International Symposium on
Imprecise Probabilities and Their Applications (ISIPTA '99, Ghent,
Belgium, 30 June - 2 July 1999, see the web site
http://ippserv.rug.ac.be/~isipta99 for more detailed information; see
http://decsai.ugr.es/~smc/isipta99/proc/proceedings.html for an
electronic version of the proceedings), we have decided to create a
biennial series of ISIPTA conferences on imprecise probabilities, each
to take place at a different location.

The Second International Symposium on Imprecise Probabilities and Their
Applications (ISIPTA '01), will be held at Cornell University, Ithaca,
NY, USA, from 26 till 29 June 2001. 

Steering Committee
------------------
Gert de Cooman (Universiteit Gent, Belgium)
Fabio G. Cozman (Universidade de Sao Paulo, Brazil)
Terrence Fine (Cornell University, USA)
Serafin Moral (Universidad de Granada, Spain)

Program Committee 
-----------------

Board:  Gert de Cooman (Belgium)

Mark Machina (USA)                      Marco Zaffalon (Switzerland)    

More information about the organising committee will appear soon on the
symposium web site.

What is imprecise probability?
------------------------------
Imprecise probability is a generic term for the many mathematical models
which measure chance or uncertainty without sharp numerical
probabilities. These models include belief functions, Choquet
capacities, comparative probability orderings, convex sets of
probability measures, fuzzy measures, interval-valued probabilities,
possibility measures, plausibility measures, and upper and lower
expectations or previsions. Such models are needed in inference problems
where the relevant information is scarce, vague or conflicting, and in
decision problems where preferences may also be incomplete. See the IPP
web site <http://ippserv.rug.ac.be> for introductory articles about
imprecise probabilities, an extensive bibliography, and a collection of
survey articles on special types of imprecise probability models.  

Symposium language
------------------
The working language of the symposium will be English. No simultaneous
translation in other languages will be available. 

How to submit a paper
---------------------
Papers are encouraged on all aspects of imprecise probability and its
applications. Those wishing to present a paper at the symposium should
submit a short paper of 4-10 pages electronically, by 15 January 2001.
LaTeX and Word style files will be made available on the symposium web
site (http://ippserv.rug.ac.be/~isipta01) well before the submission
deadline. The Program Committee will decide which of these papers are
accepted. The successful authors will then be invited to submit a final
version of their paper, for publication in a volume of symposium
proceedings (which will be available for the symposium).  

Each accepted paper will be given the opportunity for both a brief oral
presentation as well as a poster session.

All the papers that are accepted for the symposium will also be made
available on our web site (http://ippserv.rug.ac.be/~isipta01) well
before the conference. This will allow the participants to study the
papers in some detail before they are actually presented. 

Symposium web site
------------------
All information relating to the symposium will be published on the
symposium web site: http://ippserv.rug.ac.be/~isipta01

Important dates (still tentative)
---------------
Paper submission deadline:      15 January 2001
Notification of acceptance:     9 March 2001
Deadline for revised papers:    30 March 2001
Symposium:                      30 June - 2 July 1999

Questions
---------
If you have any questions about the symposium, please contact the

messages.body_plain:
And a somewhat less obscure one-liner:

mmm0[] <- format(mmm0 <- mmm, nsmall = 3)

-Don

At 11:13 AM +1000 8/27/00, Bill Venables wrote:
> At 14:47 26/08/00 -0300, Rolf Turner wrote:
> >
> >
> >I have just noticed that if you apply format() to a matrix which has
> >some NA entries, ***and*** if you give a value to the nsmall
> >argument, the result loses its matrix nature.
> >
> >E.g.:
> >
> > > mmm <- matrix(1:9/100,3,3)
> > > mmm[3,3] <- NA
> > > format(mmm)
> >       [,1]   [,2]   [,3]
> >[1,] "0.01" "0.04" "0.07"
> >[2,] "0.02" "0.05" "0.08"
> >[3,] "0.03" "0.06" "  NA"
> > > format(mmm,nsmall=3)
> >[1] "0.010" "0.020" "0.030" "0.040" "0.050" "0.060" "0.070" "0.080" "NA"
> >
> >This occurs both in Splus 3.4 and 5.1 for Unix (running under Solaris 2.7).
> >
> >Is this a bug?  Is it a known bug?
>
> Actually this seems to be one of the least consistent parts of the whole
> system.  The general question seems to be "which attributes of an argument
> does a function return in the result?"  It's not just that a general
> convention is hard to formulate and promulgate, it's that some very
> well-known functions behave very inconsistently in this respect.  For
> example if X is a matrix, why is it that sqrt(X) is a matrix with the same
> structue, but pnorm(X) is a vector?
>
> This has been annoying me for some time so I am pleased for an excuse to
> get it off my chest... :-)
>
>
> > Is there a known fix?
>
>
>
> There's always a fix, Rolf.  It just may not be what you wanted.
>
>
>
> mmm0 <- mmm
> mmm0[] <- format(mmm, nsmall = 3)
>
> or, if you want a deliberately obscure one-liner:
>
>
>
> mmm0 <- do.call("structure", c(list(format(mmm, nsmall = 3)),
> attributes(mmm)))
>
> (more seriously, this might give you a clue on how to write a suitable
> local replacement for format() that does what you want.)
>
> Bill Venables.
>
>

messages.subject: [S] Programming Challenge answered
messages.body_plain:
All,

Many thanks to Steve Smith, Bill Dunlap, Rolf Turner, Shawn Bowles, and
Bill Venables for their help.  Apparently, this was not the challenge I
thought it was!  It came down to two algorithms:

good <- x!=5 & y!=5
cor(x[good],y[good])

or

good <- !(x==5 & y==5)
cor(x[good],y[good])

The first algorithm would ignore pairs when one or the other was a 5,
which is not what I needed.  The second algorithm only ignored pairs of
5s, which is exactly what I needed.  It was easily incorporated in my
script and runs like a charm.

therefore blissfully away from email, so I missed the start of this little
discussion. :)

Speaking as an S-PLUS user who likes learning new things, I think generally
s-news works pretty well as it is.  I agree with Bill that the volume of
messages could unwieldy if everyone always replied to the whole list, and I
find the summaries very useful -- I search through the s-news archives all
the time and messages with "summary" in the title are good targets.

Yes, the MathSoft folk here do keep pretty quiet on the list (publicly at
least).  This is an independent list, thanks to the volunteers who run and
maintain it, and it's probably most useful to the community that way without
us lot trying to barge in and control everything.  But as Bill said we DO
listen, and if you've ever posted a question here chances are that among all
the responses from around the world there was also one from someone here at
S-PLUS Central in Seattle.  Suggestions and ideas raised in s-news are
common features in our development meetings.

I'll look into Stata's webseek tool.  There won't be anything as
sophisticated as that for S-PLUS 6.0, but there's always the next version.

messages.subject: [S] text rotation and spacing
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I'm plotting points that represent intervals for several discrete "units". In
the code below, index is a vector if integers 1 through n (for n units). The
vector unit.text has labels for each unit

plot(index,y,xaxt="n")
axis(1,index,labels=unit.text)

This produces equally spaced points on the x-axis and instead of a number, it
places a short label for each unit. Pretty basic. Since I may have to plot more
than 60 or so observations, the text labels get omitted when things get bunched
up. The situation is improved by using cex in the axis call, but this may cause
permanent cornea damage.

When I rotate the text 90 degrees with a call to srt in the axis function, the
labels overlap the ticks and axis so that the labels are difficult to read.

Any ideas? I think that left (or down) justification of the text would help, or
perhaps a buffer between the labels and the ticks or axis (without moving the
axis). Hopefully I haven't missed anything obvious.

Thanks in advance,

Max

messages.body_plain:
Thanks to David Brahm, Jim Pratt, Bill Dunlap and Carlisle Thacker for their
quick replies.

It turned out that the best option for my particular case is to turn off the
tick marks and use adj=1 (to right justify the text). This also allows me to
increase the font without getting to messy.

Carlisle wins the prize for the highest number of suggestions. since these may
be relavent to others in the future:

>1.  Have you tried to use larger paper?
>
>2.  Have you tried to label the even indices on axis 3 and odd on axis 1?
>    You might want all ticks on both axes.
>
>3.  Have you tried multiple calls to axis with different values of line
>    to offset labels (like suggestion 2, but everything for axis 1)?
>    You might use col to associate data with axis.
>
>4.  Have you tried to use indices for labels and a separate table to
>    associate indices (ticks) with units?
>
>5.  Have you tried to use text to put the unit labels on the plot?

Also, since I'm plotting intervals in the form of line segments, I could also
place the text on the top of the interval in rotated form.

Max

To:   s-news at wubios.wustl.edu
cc:    (bcc: Max Kuhn/BALT/BDX)
Subject:  [S] text rotation and spacing

Hello,

I'm plotting points that represent intervals for several discrete "units". In
the code below, index is a vector if integers 1 through n (for n units). The
vector unit.text has labels for each unit

plot(index,y,xaxt="n")
axis(1,index,labels=unit.text)

This produces equally spaced points on the x-axis and instead of a number, it
places a short label for each unit. Pretty basic. Since I may have to plot more
than 60 or so observations, the text labels get omitted when things get bunched
up. The situation is improved by using cex in the axis call, but this may cause
permanent cornea damage.

When I rotate the text 90 degrees with a call to srt in the axis function, the
labels overlap the ticks and axis so that the labels are difficult to read.

Any ideas? I think that left (or down) justification of the text would help, or
perhaps a buffer between the labels and the ticks or axis (without moving the
axis). Hopefully I haven't missed anything obvious.

Thanks in advance,

Max

On Mon, 28 Aug 2000, Pierre Delfosse wrote:

> 
> Dear S+ users,
> 
> I am looking for a simple approach (or function) to test for "lack of fit"
> in a linear regression with (genuine) repeated data.

The standard approach is to use anova to compare your fit with a model that
has on the rhs just a factor enumerating the repeated data.  
Something like (univariate x):

fit1 <- lm(y ~ x)
fit2 <- lm(y ~ factor(unique(x)))
anova(fit1, fit2)

messages.subject: RE: [S] Tests for lack of fit in linear regression
messages.subject_clean: [S] Tests for lack of fit in linear regression
messages.body_plain:
To S-ers:

If I may make a comment that I hope might stimulate others to respond,
preferably publicly. This is mainly an issue of experience and philosophy,
and I would like to hear what others have to say on this.

My experience has been that the standard prescription stated below by BR
generally DOES NOT WORK -- in the following sense and for the following
reasons. Generally speaking the replicate data are not true replicates in
the sense that all the sources of variability that affect results where the
explanatory variables are different are not present in the replicates. A
classical example is aliquotting in dose-respose studies. An "aliquot" is a
sample that is made up and then split among several trials (i.e.
"replicates"). Because the aliquot is formulated (dispensed) only once while
the different doses are formulated (or dispensed) separately each time, the
various sources of noise (variation in the formulation, variation in the
"plumbing" and therefore in the concentrations dispensed) present among the
different doses are NOT present (to the same degree) in the replicates. The
net effect is that the noise estimate obtained from the replicates
(severely) underestimates the true experimental variability and,
consequently, the standard statistical tests falsely proclaim lack of fit
when one what really has are different variance components. Incidentally,
for this reason, I generally distinguish between "duplicates" -- replicates
in which the noise is too low -- and "true" replicates. As Tukey emphasized,
language can be important.

As a result, my own default prescription is to look for lack of fit with
respect to a specific alternative model. That is, there is lack of fit if
the alternative fits demonstrably (statistically or in whatever other sense
you wish to define) better. I also usually replace duplicate y's by their
mean or median or some such. Of course this slightly affects at least one of
the i's in iid assumptions, but as the duplicate variance component is
usually quite small compared to the true noise, I am prepared to ignore this
nicety and proceed.

There is clearly potentially must to criticize here, so I would welcome the
views of others  -- pro or con -- practical or theoretical.

(NOTE: The views expressed here are my own and are in no way endorsed by my
company or my poor innocent colleagues at Merck).

Cheers,

Bert Gunter

messages.subject: [S] Legend VS key
messages.body_plain:
Hello S-users,

I am producing a large number of plots where I need to have two legends in the
right margin.  The first legend is just a regular legend where the different
curves are associated with the appropriate colors, line types and plotting
characters.  The second legend list some "statistics" associated with the
different curves.  To have all the plots showing a uniform appearance I find it
handy to use "legend" for both legends since legend will allow the exact
placement of the legend box by specifying the coordinates of two opposite
corners in it's x and y argument.  "Key" would be a better option for the second

same color as the associated curve, "key" also allow for a title; but the
documentation claims that "key" is more flexible than "legend", in a way it is
but in some other ways it's not, e.g. it allows specification of only one
corner, or the center or whatever, and hence their is no control on the exact
size of the key and hence it is very difficult to have more than one legend, or
key, lining up either vertically (my case) or horizontally.  Further more when
putting a border aroun a key, the border is so close of the text, at bottom and
top, that I find it looks ugly.  What about controlling space between successive
lines of text?  I find the lines are printed too close one from the other (yes I
tried changing font).

Maybe I am missing something?  Any suggestions welcome,

messages.subject: RE: [S] Tests for lack of fit in linear regression
messages.subject_clean: [S] Tests for lack of fit in linear regression
messages.body_plain:
Bert,

I understand what you are saying about tests of fit, and my experience
is similar to yours; but we need to separate out tests of statistical
hypotheses from the broader problem of evaluating scientific hypotheses.
The first is but one component of the second.

If, using the test that Brian Ripley recommended, one FAILS to reject
the hypothesis of linearity, then one knows that the observed deviations
are of the sort that COULD BE produced by chance.  This in turn indicates
that these data, in themselves, offer little or no basis for rejecting
linearity.  Used in this fashion, the test he recommended can be quite
useful.

If, on the other hand, the test rejects linearity, say, at the .01 level,
this does NOT show that the observed deviations from linearity are
reproducible.  Systematic error, of the sort that you describe in
drug testing, or of other sorts, in other fields, cannot be excluded
by the anova.  The question of whether rejection of the statistical null
hypothesis is produced by an important phenomenon or by systematic error
of obscure origin must always be considered.  I am just saying what
every experienced scientist knows.  Although occasional discussions of
this sort on s-news may be useful, I don't think Brian Ripley should
be asked to repeat such caveats every time he recommends a hypothesis test!

You recommend focussing on alternatives, in order to test linearity.
This can indeed be very useful.  If one finds a quadratic component,
for example, and in addition, over a series of studies, one sees that
the magnitude of that quadratic component varies, in a way that makes
sense in the scientific context, then of course, linearity has been
rejected rather decisively.  But the particular alternatives to linearity
that need to be explored and developed in detail vary greatly from
one context to another, and the general test suggest by Brian Ripley
is also useful, for the reasons I indicated above.  Again, the discussion
of general strategies in testing scientific hypotheses has its place,
but should not be appended to every answer that recommends a hypothesis
test!

Dave Krantz

messages.subject: [S] Dialog Box Prompts for Dataframes
messages.body_plain:
I am running S-Plus 2000 in Windows NT.  I am customising the S-Plus GUI at the 
moment, and have a dialogue box which is prompting the user for the name of a 
dataframe.  I want that box to offer me a list of the currently available 
dataframes which have a specific type of name (actually anything ending in 
".Sen.Data").

The first three lines of my script to set this up will read something like:

guiCreate("Property",
   Name = "SenDataFrame",
   DialogPrompt = "Get Data Frame",

I can now think of two ways of proceeding, but each has a problem.

(a)     From the "Widgets" example supplied with the implementation, I can use 
CopyFrom = "TXPROP_DataFrames" as the next line.  This will supply the 
currently available list, but I can't see an easy way to filter out the ones I 
don't want;

(b)     From the Programmers Guide, I can use OptionList = objects(pattern = 
"*.Sen.Data").  This one does the filtering I want, but doesn't necessarily 
give me an up-to-date list: I think it supplies the list as it was when I ran 
the program that created the dialog box.  I can update it by selecting a 
different item and then changing my mind, but this is bad programming (and I'm 
writing this for other people).

Can anyone tell me how I can by-pass this problem please?

Many thanks
David Rose

messages.subject: Re: [S] Maximum value columns in a matrix
messages.subject_clean: [S] Maximum value columns in a matrix
messages.body_plain:
Why not use names for your matrix (with dimnames), then when max is
performed, return the name of the column.
Then, you can use following function

WhereIsMax_function(N, col = T,first=T)
{
        M <- N
        dimnames(M) <- list(1:nrow(M), 1:ncol(M))
        tmp <- apply(M == max(M), 1 + indcol, sum)
        tmp2_as.numeric(names(tmp[tmp > 0]))
        if (first==T) tmp2_tmp2[1]
        return(tmp2)
}

which return the column number by default, or the row number if col=F.

Many columns may contain the maximum, so that I add a feature to return
only one number corresponding to the first column (or row) containing the
maximum.

Hopes this help

Eric

messages.subject_clean: [S] Summary: Large datasets and rounding error
messages.body_plain:
My Original Query concerned large datasets, and how
to deal with them from the point of view of cumulated
rounding error.  I got two replies.

Reply the First:

Doug Martin remarked that in Kalman filtering there
is a standard problem, to the effect that when the data set size
is so large that the data does not fit in memory, it 
becomes necessary to use recursive block-updating algorithmns.
He even gave a book,
 >Bierman, Gerald J (1977): Factorization methods for discrete sequential
>estimation, New York : Academic Press.

Reply the Second:

Albyn Jones pointed out an obvious first method (assuming
exchangeability): simply reorder the observations and
see if the coefficients change.

Many thanks to all.

Regards,

Bruce

>I have a matrix and need to find out the column with the maximum value in

Gunter, B. Biggerstaff, and C. Berry for their quick responses to my
question. Most suggestions worked for the matrix in question. The following
suggestions are my choice because of their simplicity:

messages.body_plain:
"Duncan Mackay" <Duncan.Mackay at flinders.edu.au> writes:

> Hi all, I'd like to use lme to analyze some experimental data and I would
> appreciate some feedback on setting up the appropriate formula.
> 
> I have two locations (Random blocking factor) and in each of these I have
> performed a replicated factorial experiment involving two fixed factors (say
> A and B) and a single response variable, say, Y. The data would be stored in
> Grouped Data object "mydata" with display formula Y ~ 1 | Location.
> 
> I am looking at the following formulation:-
> 
> lme(Y ~ A*B, data=mydata,
>       random = pdBlocked(list(pdIdent(~1), pdIdent(~ A - 1), pdIdent(~ B -
> )))  )
> 
> 
> Look OK??
> 
> Some worries I have are:-
> 
> Is the construction of the random formula here unnecessarily complex?
> Ridiculously so??!!
> 
> This formulation doesn't include the A*B*Location interaction - how would I
> include the latter?

The formula you have written for the random effects is appropriate for
crossed random effects.  (The computational methods in lme are highly
tuned to nested random effects rather than crossed random effects.
Although it is possible to analyze crossed random effects, it is
neither easy nor pretty.)

Your description of the experimental situation seems to indicate that
you only have random effects for Location, not for A and B.  In that
case you would call lme as
 lme(Y ~ A * B, data = mydata, random = ~ 1)
but I'm not sure you could make sense of estimating a random effect
for Location when you only have two different locations.  You may want
to consider doing a fixed-effects analysis.

I hope I have understood your problem correctly.  Please let me know
if I am misinterpreting you.
--

messages.subject: [S] censorReg() application
messages.body_plain:
S-folk,

I'm considering a possible application of censorReg() or survReg() that
falls ouside the realm of survival analysis. 

I'd like to fit regression models of the common form

Y ~ BX + e ,

For now, the description of e is not known, and (seemingly) not directly
relevant to today's question. I'd be happy using OLS or MLE methods. Either
way, I'd ultimately like to interpret the B-hats and use the model as a
predictive tool.

My practical problem is this: 

The dependent variable is concentration of an environmental chemical that
ranges from zero to some large number (say, 1000 units).  However,
measurement of very small concentrations is imperfect and therefore some
records show the dependent variable as "<DL" , where DL is a detetection
limit (say, 2 units)

censorReg() and kin seem attractive in this case because records with
response listed as y<DL could be considered "censored" observations and
specified as such in the call.

I'm concerned that this technique might be nonsensical because of the fact
that the response variable is in no sense a survival time. Do the fitting
procedures used by these functions make any sense if the response is *not* a
survival time?  Conceptually, no hazard function seems to obtain. Hmmmm.

Is there some completely other tack to take for this flavor of censored
response variables?

Any observations, suggestions, or citations would be appreciated.

Thanks
--dc

> timeseries (like a moving average except that we evaluate the maximum on a
> window instead of an average). Of course, I want to avoid the inefficient
> loop structure but the non-linear nature of the max function seems to forbid
> the use of the filter function.
> 
Try this (sent to the list rather than just privately in case there are
some refinements possible):
xmax <- 
function(x, lag) {
# lag is (window size)-1
if (lag == 1)
  return(x[1:(length(x) - 1)] + diff(x)*(diff(x) > 0))
else {
  xm <- xmax(x, lag-1)
  return(xm[1:(length(xm) - 1)] + diff(xm)*(diff(xm) > 0))
  }
}  

This beats the loop method by an order of magnitude or more and uses
significantly less memory.  [Interestingly, in R the CPU savings are not
as pronounced, the loop method is just as good with a window of 30 (when
the vector is 10000 or 100000 long).  It seems that recursion in R is
less efficient than in S-Plus, but looping is much more efficient.]

Note however that the answer is not identical to the looping method,
presumably because there are additions and subtractions involved, rather
than just comparisons.  The errors are in the order of the machine
precision.

So, YMMV!

Ray Brownrigg

messages.subject: [S] Summary: Tests for lack of fit in linear regression
messages.subject_clean: [S] Summary: Tests for lack of fit in linear regression
messages.body_plain:
Thank you very much to Siem Heisterkamp, Brian Ripley and Bill Venables for
their answers which are given hereafter for the benefit of all (some of them
were not given publicly). Answers 2+3 are essentially the same as Answer 1.

QUESTION:
 
        > Dear S+ users,
        > 
        > I am looking for a simple approach (or function) to test for "lack
of fit"
        > in a linear regression with (genuine) repeated data.

ANSWER 1:

        This simple test can be found in Draper&Smiths Linear regression.
Take
        the residuals (residual()) after the regression and do an aov(
        residuals~as.factor(x-values)). 

        Dr. S.H. Heisterkamp

ANSWER 2:

        The standard approach is to use anova to compare your fit with a
model that
        has on the rhs just a factor enumerating the repeated data.  
        Something like (univariate x):

        fit1 <- lm(y ~ x)
        fit2 <- lm(y ~ factor(x))
        anova(fit1, fit2)

        -- 
        Brian D. Ripley

ANSWER 3:

        More generally, tests of fit are no different in principle to any
        other sorts of tests.  What you do is find a larger model that
        includes the one you are testing and which in some sense is
        either trivially correct or at least much less contentious than
        yours and test yours within the larger model.  So another
        possibility for testing fit is for example

           fit2 <- lm(y ~ poly(x, 5))
           anova(fit1, fit2)

        In fact if you were to do 

           fit2 <- lm(y ~ poly(x, length(unique(x)) - 1)

        your test would be exactly the same as for the factor alternative
        given above.

        Bill Venables

messages.subject: [S] Summary: Legend VS key
messages.body_plain:
Thanks very kindly to Patrick Connely and Tim Hesterberg for their replies.
Patrick suggested, and supplied, some of his own functions to acheive what I
wanted from either legend or key.  Tim, from Mathsoft, suggested a different
approach which seems a little less involved.  I haven't tried any of the
suggestions yet, but I will in the very near future.  Following you will find
Tim's reply and at the end my original posting.

Thanks again to Patrick and Tim,

Gérald Jean
Analyste-conseil (statistiques), Actuariat
télephone            : (418) 835-4900 poste (7639)
télecopieur          : (418) 835-6657
courrier électronique: gerald.jean at spgdag.ca

"In God we trust all others must bring data"

---------------

One way to line up key's is to:
* plot the keys
  (1) with no border,
  (2) with specified x and y values, where the x values for the two keys
      are the same
  (3) centered vertically
* repeat the key() commands but with plot=F, to determine the minimum
  size of boxes needed
* draw the borders with polygon() (or lines() or segments()).
  If desired, adjust the size of the boxes to give more space above
  and below the text.

Here's some code that demonstrates the basic idea;
if you do this frequently you could write a function that handles
this for you.

plot(1:3)
key(x=1.5, y = 3, corner=c(.5, 1), text=letters[1:2], lines=list(lty=1:2))
key(x=1.5, y = 2.5, corner=c(.5, 1), text=letters[1:2], points=list(pch=1:2))
size1 <- key(x=1.5, y = 3, corner=c(.5, 1), text=letters[1:2],
lines=list(lty=1:2), plot=F)
size2 <- key(x=1.5, y = 2.5, corner=c(.5, 1), text=letters[1:2],
points=list(pch=1:2), plot=F)
polygon(x = 1.5 + max(size1[1], size2[1]) * c(-1,1,1,-1)/2 / par("uin")[1],
     y = 3   + size1[2] * c(-1,-1,0,0) / par("uin")[2],
     density=0)
polygon(x = 1.5 + max(size1[1], size2[1]) * c(-1,1,1,-1)/2 / par("uin")[1],
     y = 2.5 + size2[2] * c(-1,-1,0,0) / par("uin")[2],
     density=0)

Hope this helps.  I've also submitted an enhancement request to allow
you to specify the size.  The close border was already entered as a bug,
in our Windows version.

messages.subject: [S] Re: moving max
messages.body_plain:
> Does anyone know how to calculate efficiently a "moving max" on a timeseries
> (like a moving average except that we evaluate the maximum on a window
> instead of an average).

Ray Brownrigg wrote a beautiful recursive solution.  Here's my minor
refinement:

.window.max <- function(x, ws=1) {
  if (ws==1) return(x)
  if (ws > 2) x <- Recall(x, ws-1)
  c(NA, x[-length(x)] + pmax(0, diff(x)))
}  

My "ws" (window size) is Ray's "lag"+1.  I also padded the front with NA's, so
the result is the same length as "x".  Thanks to Bill Venables for teaching me
to recurse with "Recall".

messages.subject: [S] Re: moving max
messages.body_plain:
Well ... beauty is in the eyes of the beholder. The problem with
recursion is that it doesn't scale easily in S-Plus. Try the recursive
function on a large vector with a window of 50, say. Or with a vector of
length 100,000. Also, this is an example of what is known as "tail
recursion" - which means the recursion doesn't really add anything and can
be easily eliminated. However, for small problems and small windows, it does
just fine.

        Here is a simple for() loop version that runs about as fast or
faster and does scale (The NA's come at the end)

        mmax_function(x,ws){
        z_vector("list",ws)
        z[[1]]_x
        for(i in 2:ws){
                j_i-1
                z[[i]]_c(x[-(1:j)],rep(NA,j))
        }
        do.call("pmax",z)
        }

        I am sure that it is not the most efficient solution, but it
illustrates my point.

        Cheers,

messages.subject: [S] forcing plot### to start with 001
messages.body_plain:
When automatically exporting plots is there a way to force the plot file names
to start with plot 1?

For example
     mygraphsheet(file = "c:/graphs/plot###.wmf", format = "placeable metafile")
     .... #create a series of plots
     dev.off()

Always increments the file name, so if plot001 throught plot010 exist, then
plot011 is created.  I want to *always* start with plot001.  (The plots are
automatically imported into Word so it is less risky to write over plots than to
rely on the user to delete the old plots.)

I use S+ 2000 r2 with NT.  I'll be glad to summarize to the list.
Thanks, KJJ

messages.subject: [S] Running maximum
messages.body_plain:
Here is some running maximum code involving no recursion or looping,
explicit or implicit.  Note choice of two ways of treating NA. (If you
find the Zaslavsky approach to legibility intolerable, as many do, then
source it and print it out.)

runmax_function(x,n,na.rm=F)
{
na.code_ifelse(na.rm,-1,+1)*1e347       ### recode NA as very small/large
x[is.na(x)]_na.code
nsub_length(x)-n+1              ### number of subsequence blocks
xcol_col(matrix(0,n,nsub))
xord_xsub_xcol
xsub[]_x[c(xcol+row(xcol))-1]   ### one block per col
xord[]_order(xcol,xsub)         ### order by block and by value within block
xmax_xsub[xord[n,]]             ### pick out last of each block
xmax[xmax==na.code]_NA
xmax
}

examples:

> X
[1]  2  5  7  3 NA NA  6  4
> runmax(X,2,T)
[1]  5  7  7  3 NA  6  6
> runmax(X,2,F)
[1]  5  7  7 NA NA NA  6
